sentence: A data-driven approach based on MWD-data is likely to overcome several of these limitations: • Automated data collection from sensors provides high-resolution coverage of the entire rock mass without the need for human data assessment, addressing limitations such as 1-Human bias, 2-Inconsistent-assessment, 3-Hazardous-inspection, and 4- Non-representative-quantification. • Conceptually, the MWD-data signature can be established for small volumes, as long as there are enough MWD-values to extract a signature, say for a 1 × 1 × 1 m3 resolution, allowing for fine-grained assessment and targeted rock support, overcoming limitation 5-Not-finegrained-support. • Expanding the dataset with new features and site samples (e.g., different geo- logical conditions or tunnel uses) and retraining the cluster models is an effi- cient and transparent process, addressing limitation 6-Limited-case-studies and 7-Cumbersome-update. • Adapting the system for specific cases, such as mine junctions and tunnel openings, might be managed by adding predictive causal features to the dataset and rerunning the clustering, overcoming the limitation 8-Complex-exception-rules. • MWD-data for clustering is efficiently collected from all drillholes, from bolt- holes radially around the tunnel profile, from blasting holes ahead, and from exploratory holes ahead and outside of the profile, overcoming limitation 9-Only- visual-assessment and 10-No-advance-assessment. • A clustering approach simplifies the process of defining multiple classes, poten- tially allowing for more homogeneous rock mass material classification and targeted rock support with specific safety factors, avoiding a conservative approach with few classes, overcoming limitation 11-Non-optimised-rock-support and 12-Correct-rock- support. • The flexibility to define multiple classes, adding causal features, and tune classes to specific properties may also address limitation 13-Not-representative-failure-modes.

sentence: Elias 3 Amir Yazdanbakhsh 4 Jonathan Ragan-Kelley 1 Suvinay Subramanian 3 Michael Carbin 1 Abstract Decoding with autoregressive large language models (LLMs) traditionally occurs sequentially, generating one token after another.
label: none

sentence: An emerging line of work explored parallel decoding by identi- fying and simultaneously generating semantically independent chunks of LLM responses.
label: none

sentence: However, they rely on hand-crafted heuristics tied to syn- tactic structures like lists and paragraphs, making them rigid and imprecise.

sentence: We present PASTA, a learning-based system that teaches LLMs to iden- tify semantic independence and express parallel decoding opportunities in their own responses.

sentence: Introduction Autoregressive decoding is a fundamental efficiency bottle- neck in large language model (LLM) inference.
label: none

sentence: Contempo- rary LLMs routinely require multiple seconds or even min- utes of decoding time to complete user requests (Jiang et al., 2024; Touvron et al., 2023; Jaech et al., 2024; Daya Guo, 2025).
label: none

sentence: This latency stems from the sequential nature of autoregressive decoding, which leads to inefficient hard- ware utilization during inference.
label: research_gap

sentence: While training achieves 40-60% Model Flops Utilization (MFU) (Korthikanti et al., 2022), inference typically achieves less than 20% MFU (Pope et al., 2022).
label: research_gap

sentence: Semantic Independence.
label: none

sentence: Recent works like Skeleton-of- Thought (SoT) and APAR leverage semantic independence in LLM responses as a source of parallelism, decoding inde- pendent chunks of tokens in parallel.
label: none

sentence: Namely, these meth- ods decode semantically independent chunks (contiguous sequences of tokens) of tokens in the response in paral- lel.
label: none

sentence: Given a request, SoT first produces a bullet-point out- line, then applies regular-expression-based syntactic pattern matching to extract points that are then expanded in parallel.
label: none

sentence: APAR, in contrast, applies regular-expression-based syntac- tic pattern matching on training data to identify structures like lists and paragraphs, and finetunes an LLM to decode in parallel the item descriptions given list items and the paragraph bodies given the first sentences.
label: none

sentence: While semantic independence broadly exists in LLM re- sponses, relying purely on syntactic heuristics – manifested as hand-crafted regular expressions – to identify them has limitations.
label: research_gap

sentence: First, these heuristics lack scalability, requiring manual engineering to capture more semantic independence, even as more training compute becomes available.
label: research_gap

sentence: Second, they lack robustness, failing to detect semantic indepen- dence when responses deviate from expected patterns, even by a missing punctuation mark.
label: research_gap

sentence: These limitations moti- vate a learning-based approach to optimize LLMs’ ability to identify semantic independence, enabling LLMs to find parallelization opportunities beyond fixed patterns.
label: none

sentence: Our system consists of a set of annotations that extend the model’s vocabulary for asynchronous decoding, an interpreter that acts on these annotations to orchestrate parallel decoding, and a finetun- ing procedure that optimizes LLMs’ ability to identify and express parallelization opportunities.
label: none

sentence: Through this system, LLMs develop and execute their own asynchronous decod- ing strategies.
label: none

sentence: In Figure 1, we show how these components implement asynchronous decoding.
label: none

sentence: Our annotation language, PASTA-LANG (PArallel STructure Annotation LANGuage), enables LLMs to express semantic independence in their responses.
label: none

sentence: In Fig- ure 1, we show a PASTA-LANG-annotated response.
label: none

sentence: The <promise/> tags serve as placeholders for content chunks that are semantically independent to each other, such as ex- tracting coordinates (Tag 1 ) and recalling the line segment length formula (Tag 2 ).
label: none

sentence: Each <promise/> tag includes a topic attribute that concisely describes the chunk.
label: none

sentence: When further decoding steps require conditioning on tokens that are still being asynchronously decoded, the LLM issues an <sync/> tag to indicate so, as shown at 3 in Figure 1.
label: none

sentence: We develop the PASTA-LANG interpreter, which acts on PASTA-LANG annotations to orchestrate asyn- chronous decoding during inference.
label: none

sentence: It launches parallel decoding threads for semantically independent contents marked with <promise/> tags and synchronizes them at <sync/> tags.
label: none

sentence: The interpreter simultaneously decodes mul- tiple non-contiguous token chunks from the LLM, improv- ing overall decoding latency.
label: none

sentence: Training an LLM to generate PASTA-LANG annotations starts with two manual inputs: seven human- crafted demonstrations and a description of the PASTA- LANG annotation language.
label: none

sentence: Prompting the Gemini 1.5 Flash model (Anil et al., 2024) with these manual inputs, the PASTA system initiates an automated two-stage finetuning process.
label: none

sentence: In the first stage, PASTA uses the prompted Gemini model to create the Pasta-SFT dataset by annotating the SlimOrca instruction-finetuning dataset (Lian et al., 2023b) with PASTA-LANG annotations that identify semantically in- dependent chunks compatible with asynchronous decoding.
label: none

sentence: PASTA then finetunes an LLM on this dataset to produce a model that generates PASTA-LANG annotations.
label: none

sentence: In the second stage, PASTA creates another dataset by sam- pling the finetuned LLM and scoring each output based on its quality and latency.
label: none

sentence: Unlike traditional uses of prefer- ence optimization to improve response quality (Gui et al., 2024; Rafailov et al., 2023), we adapt one such algorithm for PASTA to optimize for both output quality and latency.
label: none

sentence: PASTA applies preference optimization to the finetuned LLM on this dataset to produce a model with improved output quality and latency.
label: none

sentence: This second stage of finetuning features a quality weight hyperparameter that controls the trade-off between quality and speedup.
label: none

sentence: Through repeated iterations of the second stage, PASTA creates models that respond with increasingly better quality and lower latency.
label: none

sentence: Varying the quality weight hyperparameter, PASTA produces a suite of models with different quality-latency trade-offs.
label: none

sentence: We evaluate these models on 805 representative instruction-following prompts from AlpacaEval (Li et al., 2023; Dubois et al., 2024).
label: none

sentence: After one iteration of prefer- ence optimization, these models Pareto-dominate all exist- ing asynchronous decoding methods.
label: none

sentence: Additional iterations of preference optimization further improve the speedup- quality Pareto frontier, showing no signs of saturation even after two iterations.
label: none

label: none

sentence: However, the prevailing practice in parallel decoding literature uses arithmetic averaging when re- porting speedup, which would show this result as 1.57-2.6×. 2 Learning to Keep a Promise Contribution.

sentence: We present a collection of contributions: • We design PASTA-LANG to be an annotation language that enables LLMs to annotate semantically independent chunks of tokens in their own responses. • We implement a PASTA-LANG interpreter that efficiently orchestrates asynchronous decoding based on PASTA- LANG annotations at inference time. • We develop a two-stage finetuning technique that trains LLMs to identify diverse patterns of semantic indepen- dence in their output and express them through PASTA- LANG annotations, while directly optimizing for both response quality and inference speedup. • We evaluate our method on AlpacaEval (Li et al., 2023; Dubois et al., 2024), a suite of 805 representa- tive instruction-following prompts, and find our method Pareto-dominate all existing asynchronous decoding meth- ods in terms of quality and speedup.
label: none

sentence: PASTA demonstrates the utility of incorporat- ing latency objectives into the standard preference optimiza- tion step during LLM post-training.
label: none

sentence: The effectiveness and scalability of this approach makes it a practical prescription for reducing LLM decoding latency. 2.
label: none

sentence: Asynchronous Decoding To provide context for how PASTA-LANG relates to other parallel decoding techniques for accelerating LLM decod- ing, we present a dichotomy of parallel decoding techniques.
label: none

sentence: Specifically, a given parallel decoding strategy can be cate- gorized as either performing synchronous or asynchronous decoding.
label: none

sentence: In synchronous decoding, only a single chunk is decoded in parallel while the rest of the generation is halted.
label: none

sentence: In contrast, during asynchronous decoding, multi- ple chunks of of the language model’s output are decoded independently in parallel.
label: none

sentence: We consider speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023; Stern et al., 2018; Cai et al., 2024; Ankner et al., 2024; He et al., 2023; Fu et al., 2024; Spector & Re, 2023; Santilli et al., 2023) as a prototypical example of synchronous decoding.
label: none

sentence: It decodes multiple tokens within a single chunk in parallel, but must complete that chunk before moving on to any subsequent tokens.
label: none

sentence: In contrast, works such as SoT (Ning et al., 2023) and APAR (Liu et al., 2024) implement asynchronous decoding techniques.
label: none

sentence: Both methods enable decoding to jump ahead in the output sequence and generate tokens before previ- ous positions are filled, resulting in multiple chunks of the output being decoded in parallel.
label: none

sentence: While our PASTA system also implements asynchronous decoding, we improve upon previous works by employing a learning-based system to identify parallelization opportunities, instead of relying on human-defined heuristics.
label: none

sentence: By training an LLM to identify and exploit parallelization opportunities, PASTA achieves Pareto-optimal trade-off between speedup and quality as compared to previous asynchronous decoding techniques. 3.
label: none

sentence: Since the model must decode content after <promise/> tags without access to the corresponding <async> content, we implement three key modifications to the standard next-token prediction finetuning algorithm.
label: none

sentence: First, the attention mask prevents the tokens after a <promise/> from attending to content within its <async> tags until a <sync/> tag is reached.

sentence: PASTA-LANG Preference Optimization.
label: none

sentence: PASTA further improves the Pasta-SFT model with a second stage of train- ing that directly optimizes for quality and speedup achieved by the PASTA-LANG annotations.
label: none

sentence: First, PASTA trains a baseline sequential model Baseline- SFT by fine-tuning the same base model on Pasta-SFT dataset without the annotations.
label: none

sentence: Then, for each prompt in the Pasta-SFT dataset, PASTA samples N different PASTA- LANG annotated responses from the Pasta-SFT model using a temperature T.
label: none

sentence: It then scores each of the N sampled re- sponses.
label: none

sentence: We set N = 10 and temperature T = 1.
label: none

sentence: The score for ranking the sampled responses is a combination of: 1.
label: none

sentence: Response theoretical speedup – the ratio between (1) the total number of tokens in Baseline-SFT’s response, and (2) the length of the longest sequence that must be decoded sequentially for Pasta-SFT’s response.
label: none

sentence: This measures the maximum achievable speedup of Pasta- SFT over Baseline-SFT. 2.
label: none

sentence: Response quality – for each sampled response, PASTA computes a confidence-weighted win-loss ratio by com- paring it against the Baseline-SFT’s response and the original SlimOrca response.
label: none

sentence: Each comparison appears in both orders and is judged by Gemini 1.5 Pro, which pro- vides a preference and a probability for that preference between 0 and 1, interpreted as confidence.
label: none

sentence: The final ratio is the confidence-weighted sum of wins divided by the confidence-weighted sum of losses.
label: none

sentence: The score for each sampled response has the following defi- nition: score = speedup+λ×quality, where λ is the quality weight hyperparameter.
label: none

sentence: For each prompt, PASTA selects the highest-scoring response as the preferred example and the lowest-scoring one as the un-preferred example.
label: none

sentence: While our methodology is compatible with any LLM prefer- ence optimization algorithm, in this work we use BoNBoN optimization (Gui et al., 2024) for it was the state-of-the-art algorithm at the time of writing this paper.
label: none

sentence: The BonBon algorithm trains a model to approximate the best-of-N re- sponse distribution by combining an SFT loss on the pre- ferred example with an IPO preference loss (Azar et al., 2024) between the best and worst response.
label: none

sentence: Specifically, the BoNBoN objective is: LBoNBoN(θ; D, θinit) = Ex,y+,y−∼D[−α log pθ(y+|x) + (1 −α)(log pθ(y+|x) pθ(y−|x) −log pθinit(y+|x) pθinit(y−|x) −1 β )2] where θ are the model weights being trained, θinit are the initial model weights, x is a prompt, y+, y−are the best and worst-of-N PASTA-LANG-annotated responses respec- tively, and α is a hyperparameter to weight the SFT and IPO loss contributions.
label: none

sentence: We set θinit to be the Pasta-SFT model.
label: none

sentence: We use a learning rate of 5E-7 and set α to 0.005 as recommended by (Gui et al., 2024). 5.
label: none

sentence: Experiment We evaluated the performance of our PASTA-LANG- equipped model in terms of speedup, parallelism, and re- sponse quality and show that it is Pareto-optimal compared to other asynchronous decoding techniques. 5.1.

sentence: Positional Embedding Asynchronous decoding methods introduce uncertainty over the true position of tokens as they are being generated as the output is generated in a non-sequential manner.
label: research_gap

sentence: Namely, the main decoding thread is unaware of the true length of of any previously occurring <async> blocks that have not been synchronized.
label: none

sentence: Thus, the main thread must estimate the number of tokens in an <async> block before contin- uing generation.
label: none

sentence: If the predicted number of tokens for the <async> block does not match the true number of tokens generated, this can lead to errors as the position IDs af- ter synchronization will either not increase monotonically (predicted too few) or contain a gap (predicted too many).
label: none

sentence: To minimize the error between the true and predicted position IDs, we compare three different ap- proaches for position ID assignment: Fixed-length: We make the assumption that each <async> block has a fixed length.

sentence: PASTA-LANG Preference Score When performing PASTA-LANG preference optimization, we compute a preference score for each PASTA-LANG anno- tated response as a weighted combination of a quality term and a decoding efficiency term, which is meant to reflect the improvement in decoding speed for a response.
label: none

sentence: While our ultimate goal is to increase decoding speed, it is not ob- vious a priori that directly optimizing for the speedup will produce the desired behavior.
label: none

sentence: Such an objective could lead to degenerate solutions such as producing short responses.
label: none

sentence: To determine the most performant decoding efficiency term, we investigate four separate metrics for the decoding efficiency of a response: (a) the theoretical speedup of the response only (b) the harmonic mean of the theoretical speedup and theoretical parallelism of the response (c) the arithmetic mean of the theoretical speedup and theoretical parallelism of the response (d) the theoretical parallelism of the response only.
label: none

sentence: We re-compute the preference score for each training re- sponse using each of the efficiency metrics we present above.
label: none

sentence: We then perform a single round of BoNBoN training on each of the different preference labeled datasets.
label: none

sentence: Figure 5 (Right) presents the response quality and speedup for each model trained to optimize a different de- coding efficiency metric.
label: none

sentence: Intuitively, one might expect the harmonic mean to be the most effective since it encourages balanced optimization by inducing a larger weight on the weaker metric.
label: none

sentence: However, we find that optimizing for har- monic mean performs similarly to optimizing directly for speedup.
label: none

sentence: We hypothesize this is because our LLM-based quality evaluation naturally favors longer, more detailed responses, preventing the model from artificially increasing speedup through response truncation.
label: limitation

sentence: As expected, optimiz- ing solely for theoretical parallelism leads to poor speedup, demonstrating the importance of including speedup in the objective.
label: none

sentence: Based on these results, we adopted theoretical speedup only as our efficiency metric. 9 Learning to Keep a Promise 7.

sentence: Agent Planning/Tool Use.
label: none

sentence: Our work is related to the idea of agent planning and tool use (Yao et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2023).
label: none

sentence: Prior studies show that LLM-based agents can solve complex tasks by planning and using tools such as web search and external APIs.
label: none

sentence: Our work extends the suite of tools available to LLMs with the PASTA-LANG language and interpreter for improving their own decoding efficiency.
label: none

sentence: Approximate Parallelization.
label: none

sentence: Our work extends the idea of approximate parallelization (Udupa et al., 2011; Misailovic et al., 2012).
label: none

sentence: Udupa et al. (2011) proposed a framework that enables programmers to annotate breakable data dependen- cies in a program and developed a compiler and runtime that exploits these annotations to automatically parallelize oth- erwise sequential regions of code.
label: none

sentence: Misailovic et al. (2012) opportunistically relaxes synchronization primitives in a par- allel program to improve parallelism, to program outputs that are acceptably close to the original one.
label: none

sentence: Similarly, we break the sequential decoding process of LLMs into ap- proximately parallelizable and independent components and exploit the parallelism to improve decoding efficiency.
label: none

sentence: Our work differs in that instead of relying on end-user annota- tion or compiler analysis, we teach LLMs to autonomously express parallelism in their own decoding process using the PASTA-LANG annotation language. 8.
label: none

sentence: Conclusion We present PASTA, a system that teaches LLMs to identify semantically independent chunks in their own responses and annotate them for parallel decoding opportunities.
label: none

sentence: Through a set of annotations, an interpreter and a finetuning proce- dure, our method enables learned asynchronous decoding.
label: none

sentence: PASTA is an effective and scalable system which enables learned asynchronous decoding.
label: none

sentence: Evalua- tion on AlpacaEval demonstrates that our approach Pareto- dominates existing asynchronous decoding methods in terms of quality and speedup.
label: none

sentence: The improvements continue with additional training compute, showing no signs of satu- ration during our experimental evaluation.
label: none

sentence: LARS Optimizer Standard Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD)[9] uses same Learning Rate (LR) in each layer.
label: none

sentence: The problems are two-fold.
label: none

sentence: Firstly, if the learning rate is small, the conver- gence of training might take too much time.
label: none

sentence: Sometimes, it might not even converge.
label: none

sentence: Secondly, if the learning rate is high, the training process might end up with under-ﬁtting of the model.
label: none

sentence: In order to prevent under-ﬁtting, the initial phase of training should be highly sensitive to the weight initial- ization and initial learning rate[11].
label: none

sentence: LARS[11] claims that the L2-norm of weights and gradients varies signiﬁcantly between weights and biases, and between different layers.
label: none

sentence: Training might become unstable if learning rate is large compared to this ratio in some layers.
label: none

sentence: In order to solve this problem, there is a popular approach called learning rate warm-up.
label: none

sentence: This approach starts with a small learning rate which can be used for any layer and slowly increases the learning rate.
label: none

sentence: Instead of maintaining a single global learning rate, LARS maintains separate local learning rate for each layer.
label: none

sentence: Equation 1 is used to calculate the weight using the local and global learning rate. ∆wl t = γ ∗λl ∗∇L(wt) (1) In Equation 1, γ is the global learning rate and λl is the layer-wise local learning rate.
label: none

sentence: Local learning rate for each layer is deﬁned through a trust co-efﬁcient which is much smaller than 1.
label: none

sentence: Trust co-efﬁcient deﬁnes how much a layer can be trusted to change its weight during update.
label: none

sentence: Local learning rate can be calculated using Equation 2. λl = η ∗ ||wl|| ||∇L(wl)|| (2) In Equation 2, η is the trust coefﬁcient.
label: none

sentence: In case of Stochastic Gradient Descent, a term known as weight decay[8] can be used.
label: none

sentence: Equation for calculating local learning rate can also be extended to balance the learning rate with weight decay according to Equation 3. λl = η ∗ ||wl|| ||∇L(wl)|| + β ∗||wl|| (3) In Equation 3, β is the weight decay term.
label: none

sentence: An In-depth Investigation of Sparse Rate Reduction in Transformer-like Models Yunzhe Hu School of Computing and Data Science The University of Hong Kong yzhu@cs.hku.hk Difan Zou School of Computing and Data Science & Institute of Data Science The University of Hong Kong dzou@cs.hku.hk Dong Xu School of Computing and Data Science The University of Hong Kong dongxu@cs.hku.hk Abstract Deep neural networks have long been criticized for being black-box.

sentence: To unveil the inner workings of modern neural architectures, a recent work [45] proposed an information-theoretic objective function called Sparse Rate Reduction (SRR) and interpreted its unrolled optimization as a Transformer-like model called Coding Rate Reduction Transformer (CRATE).
label: none

sentence: However, the focus of the study was primarily on the basic implementation, and whether this objective is optimized in practice and its causal relationship to generalization remain elusive.
label: research_gap

sentence: Going beyond this study, we derive different implementations by analyzing layer-wise behaviors of CRATE, both theoretically and empirically.
label: none

sentence: To reveal the predictive power of SRR on generalization, we collect a set of model variants induced by varied implementations and hyperparameters and evaluate SRR as a complexity measure based on its correlation with generalization.
label: none

sentence: Surprisingly, we find out that SRR has a positive correlation coefficient and outperforms other baseline measures, such as path-norm and sharpness-based ones.
label: none

sentence: Furthermore, we show that generalization can be improved using SRR as regularization on benchmark image classification datasets.
label: none

sentence: We hope this paper can shed light on leveraging SRR to design principled models and study their generalization ability. 1 Introduction Transformers [39, 11] have become the de facto choice of neural architecture nowadays and find great success in applications across language, vision, speech, and other scientific fields.
label: none

sentence: The self-attention module in Transformers utilize global interactions to capture long-range dependency.
label: none

sentence: However, the mechanisms and learning process of self-attention and other components in Transformers remain open problems, calling for more research to interpret and understand their properties.
label: research_gap

sentence: One approach to interpreting the attention module involves experimental observation of the attention module to gain insights into their behaviors.
label: none

sentence: For instance, DINO [7] provides a means to observe and analyze attention maps w.r.t class tokens in Vision Transformer (ViT), shedding light on their emerging interpretability from self-supervised learning.
label: none

sentence: Another line of work focuses on interpreting or building attention module and even Transformer-like models from a mathematical perspective.
label: none

sentence: Works in this vein have attempted to establish connections between Transformers and a reverse-engineered energy 38th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2024). arXiv:2411.17182v1 [cs.LG] 26 Nov 2024 function [43, 17], associative memory such as modern Hopfield network [35, 37, 26, 4] and sparse distributed memory [5], or programming languages [41, 22], to name a few.
label: none

sentence: Recently, the study of algorithm unrolling has emerged as a promising technique to bridge the gap between iterative optimization and neural architecture.
label: none

sentence: A work by Yu et al. [45] considers the objective of representation learning as optimizing the Sparse Rate Reduction (SRR), a function that promotes maximum information gain described by the coding rate function [24, 46] and induces sparsity.
label: none

sentence: In particular, they show that a Multi-head Subspace Self-Attention (MSSA) operator with skip connection and an Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding Algorithms (ISTA) operator can be derived under some assumptions by unrolling minimization of the coding rate of representations in incoherent subspaces, i.e., compression and sparse coding, i.e., sparsification, respectively.
label: none

sentence: By stacking these operations into layers, they build a Transformer-like model CRATE in which every layer should have the completely interpretable compress-then-sparsify behavior.
label: none

sentence: However, although motivated by an information-theoretic and principled objective, it is still unexplored whether the core component MSSA operator with skip connection indeed implements the idea of compression in practice and how information propagates in the forward pass.
label: research_gap

sentence: On the other hand, SRR as the objective of representation learning is still an empirical formulation.
label: research_gap

sentence: Its causal relationship to generalization remains elusive.
label: research_gap

sentence: In this paper, we conduct an in-depth investigation of this Transformer-like model and take steps to address these limitations.
label: none

sentence: Our contributions are summarized as follows: • In Section 4, we highlight the derivation artifacts through analysis of the key component MSSA operator and explore implementation variants of CRATE by inspecting the layer-wise behaviors.
label: none

sentence: We show that the gradient approximation of the compression term will yield a counterproductive effect, performing decompression of token representations instead. • In Section 5, we uncover the correlation between the learning objective SRR and generalization in unrolled models.
label: none

sentence: By training models with varied hyperparameters, we show that SRR as a complexity measure has a positive correlation coefficient and outperforms other baselines. • In Section 6, we demonstrate the effectiveness of SRR as a regularization technique for improved performance on benchmark datasets.
label: none

sentence: Specifically, we show that the classification accuracy of unrolled models on CIFAR-10/100 can be consistently improved using a simple and efficient implementation of regularization. 2 Related Work 2.1 Interpreting Transformers Research on interpreting Transformers [39, 11] has surged recently.

sentence: Despite its achievements, the mechanisms and learning of attention layers remain enigmatic.

sentence: One approach to interpreting Transformers is to experimentally observe the inner representations or output of key components like self-attention.

sentence: This includes analysis by projecting parameters of Transformers to embedding space [10], inspecting the representations with another language model [14], visualizing attention map [7, 8, 44], etc. Several works opt for “mechanistic interpretability” [12, 28, 40] aiming to reverse- engineer the representations learned by Transformers that have “grokked” or mastered complex modular arithmetic task [34] and other synthetic tasks [23, 47].

sentence: Although designed with a principled objective, we identify an artifact in its forward construction and show that the simplest implementation can have the opposite effect in realizing its designed goal.

sentence: Limitations This study has several limitations.
label: limitation

sentence: Firstly, the conclusion that the SRR measure can be a strong indicator of generalization is limited to the CRATE family.
label: limitation

sentence: Generalizing this conclusion to standard Transformers would be non-trivial, as the SRR measure is not properly defined when the query- key-value matrices have independent learnable parameters instead of shared ones.
label: limitation

sentence: Secondly, the performance of a more faithful implementation (CRATE-N) falls behind the one with a simple manipulation (CRATE-T).
label: limitation

sentence: This calls for a rigorous inspection of each component’s functionality in the framework.
label: future_work

sentence: Lastly, while we confirm the positive correlation to generalization, our analysis is limited in scale.
label: limitation

sentence: Consequently, drawing definitive conclusions regarding whether SRR can be a principle or necessitates further engineering to push the model’s limit is challenging.
label: limitation

sentence: A Better and more systematic way is needed to determine whether SRR is principled for designing the Transformer- like models and quantify this relationship in an appropriate task, perhaps beyond classification.

sentence: Introduction Deep learning has achieved success in a wide variety of problems, ranging from time- series data to images and video [1].
label: none

sentence: Data from these tasks are referred to as Euclidean [2] and specialised models such as recurrent and convolutional neural networks [3,4] have been designed to leverage the properties of such data.
label: none

sentence: Despite these successes, not all problems are Euclidean.
label: none

sentence: One particular class of such problems involve graphs, which naturally model complex real-world settings involving objects and their relationships.
label: none

sentence: Recently, deep learning approaches have been extended to graph-based domains using graph neural networks (GNNs) [5], which leverage certain topological structures and properties speciﬁc to graphs [2].
label: none

sentence: Since graphs comprise entities and the relationships between them, GNNs are said to learn relational information and may have the ability for relational reasoning [6].
label: none

sentence: One reason for the success of deep learning models is their ability to transfer to new tasks.
label: none

sentence: In image classiﬁcation, this transfer leads to more robust models and faster training [7].
label: none

sentence: Despite the importance of transfer in deep learning, there has been little insight into the nature of transferring relational knowledge — that is, the representations learnt by graph neural networks.
label: research_gap

sentence: There is also no comparison of the generalisability of different GNNs when evaluated on downstream task performance.
label: research_gap

sentence: This lack of insight is in part due to the lack of a model-agnostic and task-agnostic framework and standard benchmark datasets and tasks for carrying out transfer learning experiments with GNNs.
label: research_gap

sentence: We conduct an empirical study within the contexts of node classiﬁcation and graph classiﬁcation to determine whether transfer in GNNs occur and, if so, what factors inﬂuence success.
label: none

sentence: In particular, we make the following contributions: First, we provide a methodol- ogy and additional metrics for evaluating GNN transfer learning empirically.
label: none

sentence: Second, we arXiv:2202.00740v1 [cs.LG] 1 Feb 2022 2 of 20 provide a novel method for creating synthetic graph classiﬁcation tasks with community structure.
label: none

sentence: Finally, we evaluate the transferability of several popular GNNs on both real and synthetic datasets.
label: none

sentence: Our results demonstrate that we can achieve positive transfer using graph neural networks; and that certain models exploit strong community structure properties present in the source task to yield effective transfer. 1.1.

sentence: Background In this work, we consider problems for which the data can be modelled as a graph.
label: none

sentence: A graph G = {V, E} consists of a set of N vertices, V, and a set of edges E.
label: none

sentence: Let vi ∈V denote a vertex, and eij = (vi, vj) ∈E denote a directed edge from vi to vj.
label: none

sentence: The adjacency matrix, A ∈RN×N, has aij = 1 where eij ∈E, and 0 otherwise.
label: none

sentence: A graph may have node attributes, where X ∈RN×C is the node feature matrix, and xi ∈RC is the attribute vector for node vi.
label: none

sentence: Similarly, a graph may have an edge attribute matrix Xe [5].
label: none

sentence: An important measure of a node’s connectivity is its degree, which is the number of edges the node is connected to [8].
label: none

sentence: We denote the degree of the ith node as di.
label: none

sentence: The degree matrix D = diag(d1, . . . , dN) is the diagonal matrix containing the degrees of all vertices. 1.1.1.
label: none

sentence: Graph Neural Networks The success of CNNs for computer vision problems motivate the need to formulate a counterpart to the convolution operator for graphs [2].
label: none

sentence: Similarly to that of Euclidean signals, the problem of convolution for graphs can be tackled from either the spatial domain or spectral domain.
label: none

sentence: One popular model is Graph Convolution Networks (GCNs) [9], which make use of a spectral graph convolution operation stacked layer-wise.
label: none

sentence: We also consider two other models, GraphSAGE [10] and Graph Isomorphism Networks (GINs) [11], which utilise spatial graph convolutions to aggregate information from a node’s neighbourhood.
label: none

sentence: GINs have previously outperformed both GCN and GraphSAGE in experimental performance on social media and biological datasets [11].
label: none

sentence: These three considered GNNs fall under the category of message-passing neural networks (MPNNs) [12].
label: none

sentence: Transfer Learning Deep neural network and machine learning models are usually trained for a speciﬁc task from a random initialisation of their parameters.
label: none

sentence: If the task or nature of the input data changes, the network must be retrained from scratch.
label: none

sentence: This retraining differs from humans, who reuse past knowledge and apply it to new contexts and tasks.
label: none

sentence: The ability to reuse knowledge beyond the context in which it was learnt is known as transfer learning [13].
label: none

sentence: Transfer with neural networks can be achieved by simply reusing a previously-trained network’s weights.
label: none

sentence: The transferred weights can either be used as a starting point for training a network (ﬁne-tuned transfer), or used as ﬁxed features on the target task (frozen-weight transfer).
label: none

sentence: To formalise transfer learning, Pan and Yang [14] deﬁne the notion of domains and tasks as used in this paper.
label: none

sentence: Taylor and Stone [13] present various metrics for the evaluation of transfer learning, including Transfer Ratio, Jumpstart and Asymptotic Performance.
label: none

sentence: The Transfer Ratio is the ratio of the total cumulative performance of the transfer learner to the base learner, while Jumpstart is the initial performance improvement by the transfer over the base learner.
label: none

sentence: Synthetic Data For meaningful classiﬁcations, instances within a single class should be similar.
label: none

sentence: A graph where nodes in the same class are densely connected is said to contain strong community structure.
label: none

sentence: The Modularity, deﬁned as M = 1 2|E| ∑ ij  aij −didj 2|E|  δ(i, j), is one measure of a graph’s community structure with respect to the structure of the network [32], where δ(i, j) = 1 if vi and vj belong to the same class, and 0 otherwise.
label: none

sentence: The Within Inertia ratio is another measure of the community structure that takes into account node attribute values [33].
label: none

sentence: Given a partition of the graph’s vertices P, the Within Inertia is given by: I = ∑ C∈P ∑ v∈C dist(xv, gC)2 ∑ v∈V dist(xv, g)2 , 5 of 20 where dist(xvi, xvj) is the Euclidean distance between node attribute vectors, gC is the centre of gravity of the vertices in C, and g the global centre of gravity of all vertices.

sentence: To generate synthetic datasets, we make use of DANCer: a generator for dynamic attributed networks with community structure [33].
label: none

sentence: The generator produces graphs with communities using micro-operations (local operations such as removing a node) and macro- operations (community-level operations such as splitting a community).
label: none

sentence: The generator is designed with both structural and attribute homophily [34] in mind.
label: none

sentence: It also models phenomena such as preferential attachment, where nodes are more likely to connect with nearby or highly connected nodes [35].
label: none

sentence: These properties make DANCer an ideal generator for our purposes.

sentence: Graph Classiﬁcation Experimental Design Graph classiﬁcation is the problem of categorising whole graphs.
label: none

sentence: We follow the same experimental procedure as for node classiﬁcation.

sentence: We want to evaluate whether a dataset contains graphs with community structure at a graph-level.
label: none

sentence: With this aim, we present an extension of the concept of community structure from node to graph level for both structural and attribute properties.
label: none

sentence: The Within Inertia is a general measure of community structure since it does not depend on graph-theoretic 7 of 20 properties, but only on the Euclidean distance between data points.
label: none

sentence: Given a dataset D, and a partition of classes P, a general form of the Within Inertia can be written as: ∑ C∈P ∑ i∈C dist(ρi, gC)2 ∑ i∈D dist(ρi, g)2 , (1) where ρi is a graph property we are interested in measuring for graph i in class C, gC is the centre of gravity of the graphs in C, and g is the global center of gravity of all the graphs.
label: none

sentence: The Euclidean distance dist(·) may be replaced by other distance metrics if the generation process is unknown [38,39].
label: none

sentence: We replace ρi in the Eq. 1 with any property we want to measure community structure for.
label: none

sentence: For attribute community structure we substitute the mean of each graph’s attribute matrix, ¯X, for ρi: IA = ∑ C∈P ∑ i∈C dist . ¯Xi, gC 2 ∑ i∈D dist . ¯Xi, g 2 .
label: none

sentence: There is no consensus on how to approach structural community structure.
label: research_gap

sentence: There are numerous ways of measuring graph similarity [40], the most common being graph-edit distance [41].
label: none

sentence: Another approach is to compare graph spectra.
label: none

sentence: However, these methods are slow to compute and are thus not useful for measuring entire datasets with multiple graphs.
label: research_gap

sentence: Modularity takes node degrees as a valuable property for determining community structure for nodes.
label: none

sentence: Since we want to measure community structure at the graph level, we use the average node degree for a graph.
label: none

sentence: We substitute the average node degree, ¯di, for ρi in Eq. 1.
label: none

sentence: This serves as the structural community structure measure for our datasets: IS = ∑ C∈P ∑ i∈C dist . ¯di, gC 2 ∑ i∈D dist . ¯di, g 2 . 2.2.1.

sentence: To create a meaningful graph classiﬁcation task, we parameterise a generator to control the community structure for both structure and attributes.
label: none

sentence: To do this, we generate the dataset using the following four steps: 1.
label: none

sentence: Create a random n-class classiﬁcation problem with a sample X and labels y. 2.
label: none

sentence: For each label yi in y, generate several graphs and set their node attributes to the relevant example from X.
label: none

sentence: Label these graphs with yi. 3.
label: none

sentence: Optionally, swap the labels assigned to some of the graphs to weaken community structure. 4.
label: none

sentence: Optionally, replace node attributes with noise to weaken attribute community struc- ture.
label: none

sentence: Steps 1 and 2 create community structure for attributes and structure respectively, and the ﬁnal two steps weaken the community structure if selected to do so.
label: none

sentence: Figure 2 illustrates this process, where the blue blocks create community structure and the pink blocks weaken it.

sentence: Discussion Our research presented several contributions for understanding transfer learning using graph neural networks.
label: none

sentence: We proposed a framework for evaluating transfer with GNNs by testing various source tasks on a ﬁxed target task.
label: none

sentence: We employed this framework, along with transfer learning metrics and notions of community structure, to evaluate the transferability of three useful GNNs: GCN, GraphSAGE and GIN.
label: none

sentence: We tested and compared these models using real-world and synthetic graph data for node classiﬁcation and graph classiﬁcation contexts.
label: none

sentence: In addition, we presented a novel procedure for generating synthetic datasets for graph classiﬁcation.
label: none

sentence: All three of the GNNs we selected can transfer knowledge across training on the target task.
label: none

sentence: GCN and GIN can exploit Strong Modularity in the source task, while GraphSAGE can leverage both structural and attribute information for node classiﬁcation.
label: none

sentence: Conclusions This research begins to standardise the procedure and metrics for evaluating transfer learning using GNNs.
label: none

sentence: Research on deep learning with graphs is expanding rapidly, and understanding how we can achieve effective transfer is therefore of great beneﬁt.

sentence: Approximation Power of Deep Neural Networks An explanatory mathematical survey Owen Davis∗1 and Mohammad Motamed†2 1Department of Optimization & Uncertainty Quantification, Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, USA 2Department of Mathematics and Statistics, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, USA Dedicated to Raúl Tempone Abstract This survey provides an in-depth and explanatory review of the approximation properties of deep neural networks, with a focus on feed-forward and residual architectures.
label: none

sentence: The primary objec- tive is to examine how effectively neural networks approximate target functions and to identify conditions under which they outperform traditional approximation methods.
label: none

sentence: Key topics include the nonlinear, compositional structure of deep networks and the formalization of neural network tasks as optimization problems in regression and classification settings.
label: none

sentence: The survey also addresses the training process, emphasizing the role of stochastic gradient descent and backpropagation in solving these optimization problems, and highlights practical considerations such as activation functions, overfitting, and regularization techniques.
label: none

sentence: Additionally, the survey explores the density of neural networks in the space of continuous functions, comparing the approximation capabilities of deep ReLU networks with those of other approximation methods.
label: none

sentence: It discusses recent theoretical advancements in understanding the expressiveness and limitations of these networks.
label: none

sentence: A detailed error-complexity analysis is also presented, focusing on error rates and computational complexity for neural networks with ReLU and Fourier-type activation functions in the context of bounded target functions with minimal regularity assumptions.
label: none

sentence: Alongside recent known results, the survey introduces new findings, offering a valuable resource for understanding the theoretical founda- tions of neural network approximation.
label: none

sentence: Concluding remarks and further reading suggestions are provided. keywords: approximation theory of neural networks, mathematics of deep learning, constructive approximation, error-complexity analysis Intended audience.
label: none

sentence: The material in this survey should be accessible to undergraduate and grad- uate students, as well as researchers in mathematics, statistics, computer science, and engineering.

62 3 Prologue: What this survey is and is not about Three key questions about deep neural networks, in the context of approximation, include: 1.
label: none

sentence: Approximation Theory: Given a target function space and a neural network architecture, what is the best the network can do in approximating the target function?
label: none

sentence: Are there function spaces where certain neural network architectures outperform other methods of approximation? 2.
label: none

sentence: Optimal Experimental Design: Given a target function space, how can we effectively design the network architecture and generate data samples—by identifying and sampling from an optimal distribution—to achieve the best or near-best approximation with minimal compu- tational effort? 3.
label: none

sentence: Learning Process: Given a neural network architecture and a data set, how can we efficiently train generalizable networks, and when do optimization techniques like stochastic gradient descent work?
label: none

sentence: Are there alternatives to gradient-based optimization methods?
label: none

sentence: This survey focuses solely on the first question, offering an explanatory review of deep networks’ approximation properties.
label: none

sentence: It is structured into three chapters: • Chapter 1 introduces key concepts in deep networks, their compositional structure, and formalizes the neural network problem as an optimization problem for regression and clas- sification.
label: none

sentence: The chapter also briefly discusses stochastic gradient descent, backpropagation, activation functions, cost functions, overfitting, and regularization. • Chapter 2 reviews the density of neural networks in the space of continuous functions.
label: none

sentence: Starting with the concept of density in polynomial approximation, it explores the ability of feedforward networks to approximate continuous functions, including recent advances on deep ReLU networks’ approximation capabilities. • Chapter 3 focuses on error-complexity analysis, covering estimates for ReLU and Fourier- activated networks, with an emphasis on results for bounded target functions under minimal regularity assumptions.
label: none

sentence: We aim to provide an accessible yet rigorous explanatory review, balancing foundational in- sights with advanced topics.
label: none

sentence: To achieve this, the chapters are structured to progressively increase in complexity, accommodating a broad audience that includes senior undergraduates, graduate students, and advanced researchers.
label: none

sentence: While our focus is on key concepts and techniques, particu- larly those related to (residual) feed-forward networks with rectified linear and complex exponential activations, this survey is not an exhaustive account of all network types, architectures, or ap- proximation estimates.
label: limitation

sentence: Notable exclusions include popular architectures such as convolutional networks, sinusoidal representation networks, and Fourier neural operators, as well as advanced mathematical tools like Rademacher complexity.
label: limitation

sentence: Instead, our goal is to present a clear and focused narrative that illuminates the fundamental mechanisms driving the success of deep networks, while staying within the constraints of scope and length.
label: none

sentence: The survey concludes with Chapter 4, which offers further reading and final remarks. 4 Chapter 1: Neural networks: formalization and key concepts This chapter introduces the key ideas and concepts underlying feed-forward neural networks in the context of supervised learning, applied to regression and classification tasks.
label: none

sentence: It begins by outlining the compositional nonlinear structure of feed-forward networks and formulates the network problem as an optimization task.
label: none

sentence: Next, it discusses the (stochastic) gradient descent algorithm and presents the backpropagation formulas used for solving the optimization problem.
label: none

sentence: Finally, the chapter covers various topics concerning the performance of neural networks, including activation and cost functions, overfitting, and regularization. 1 Feed-forward neural networks An L-hidden layer feed-forward neural network (NN) is a parametric map fθ : Rd →RnL with parameters θ ∈Rnθ, formed by the composition of L + 1 ≥2 maps fθ(x) = f L ◦· · · ◦f 1 ◦f 0(x), x ∈Rd.
label: none

sentence: (1) Each individual map f ℓ: Rnℓ−1 →Rnℓ, with ℓ= 0, 1, . . . , L, and n−1 = d, forms one layer of the network and is given by the component-wise application of a nonlinear activation function σℓto a multidimensional affine map, f ℓ(z) = σℓ(M ℓz + bℓ), z ∈Rnℓ−1, M ℓ∈Rnℓ×nℓ−1, bℓ∈Rnℓ, ℓ= 0, 1, . . . , L.
label: none

sentence: (2) The weight matrices {M ℓ}L ℓ=0 and bias vectors {bℓ}L ℓ=0 together form the network parameter vector θ = {(M ℓ, bℓ)}L ℓ=0.
label: none

sentence: The total number of network parameters is then calculated as nθ = PL ℓ=0 nℓ(nℓ−1 +1).
label: none

sentence: Given a set of activation functions, a neural network is uniquely determined by its parameter vector.
label: none

sentence: The network parameters are tuned during a process referred to as training so that fθ accomplishes a prescribed regression or classification task; we will discuss the training process in Sections 3-4.
label: none

sentence: The compositional structure of a network, given in (1)-(2), can be illustrated by a graph.
label: none

sentence: As an example, Figure 1 depicts a graph representation of a feed-forward network with L = 7 hidden layers and specific neuron counts: d = 2, n0 = 3, n1 = n2 = n3 = n4 = n5 = 4, n6 = 2, n7 = 1.
label: none

sentence: Figure 1: Graph representation of a feed-forward network with L = 7 hidden layers, and two input and one output neuron.
label: none

sentence: The number of neurons in hidden layers varies between 2 and 4. 5 In a graph representation, nodes correspond to neurons arranged in layers, while edges represent connections linking neurons across adjacent layers, with each edge indicating a scalar weight multiplication.
label: none

sentence: Specifically, the network graph consists of an input layer with d nodes, an output layer with nL nodes, and L hidden layers with n0, n1, . . . , nL−1 nodes, respectively.
label: none

sentence: Input neurons receive the d components of the independent variable vector x = (x1, . . . , xd), while output neurons generate the nL components of fθ = (fθ,1, . . . , fθ,nL).
label: none

sentence: We define the “architecture" of a network by considering the number of layers, neurons, and their corresponding activation functions.
label: none

sentence: The number of hidden layers L in a network determines its “depth"; in general, a higher L indicates a deeper network.
label: none

sentence: The number of neurons nℓin each layer ℓdetermines the “width" of that layer and, consequently, the overall width of the network.
label: none

sentence: Increasing the number of network parameters nθ can be achieved by making the network wider, deeper, or both.
label: none

sentence: It is worth noting that different layers within a network can have varying numbers of neurons and use different activation functions.
label: none

sentence: For networks with a uniform width W, where nℓ= W for ℓ= 0, 1, . . . , L −1, we find that nθ scales approximately as LW 2.
label: none

sentence: In other words, the number of network parameters increases linearly with the depth L and quadratically with the width W. 2 Applications of neural networks Neural networks, particularly in supervised learning, are extensively employed for solving two main types of problems: regression and classification.
label: none

sentence: Regression: In multivariate regression, we aim to build a mapping fθ : Rd →RnL, given a set of input-output data {(x(m), y(m))}n m=1 ∈Rd × RnL.
label: none

sentence: This mapping should approximate y(m) for x(m), without overfitting, ensuring good performance beyond the provided dataset; see Section 7 for a discussion on overfitting.
label: none

sentence: Function approximation is a specific instance of regression, where we aim to approximate a target function f : Rd →RnL using a dataset (x(m), f(x(m))) n m=1.
label: none

sentence: In other words, our objective is to find a network fθ such that fθ(x) ≈f(x).
label: none

sentence: Classification.
label: none

sentence: In multi-classification, data are categorized into nL distinct classes, labeled as c1, . . . , cnL.
label: none

sentence: Given an input dataset {x(m)}n m=1 ∈Rd, such as a set of images, with their cor- responding class labels {c(m)}n m=1, where c(m) ∈{c1, . . . , cnL}, the objective is to construct a mapping fθ : Rd →[0, 1]nL that provides the posterior probabilities of class membership for a given pattern x ∈Rd, such as an image.
label: none

sentence: In other words, we aim to find a network fθ such that fθ(x) ≈(Prob(c1|x), . . . , Prob(cnL|x)). 3 Network training as an optimization problem Network training is the process of finding or tuning the parameters of a network.
label: none

sentence: Given n pairs of input-output training data points {(x(m), y(m))}n m=1, the objective is to train a network with a predefined architecture to learn the underlying function from the available training data.
label: none

sentence: This entails finding a parametric map fθ : Rd →RnL, where θ = {(W ℓ, bℓ)}L ℓ=1 represents the network parameters, such that fθ(x) approximates the target y.
label: none

sentence: This is done by minimizing a specified loss (or empirical risk) function, denoted by Rn, that measures the “distance” between fθ(x) and 6 y for the training data set.
label: none

sentence: Training can thus be formulated as an optimization problem: find θ as the solution of min θ Rn(θ), Rn(θ) = 1 n n X m=1 Cm(θ), Cm(θ) = C(y(m), fθ(x(m))).
label: none

sentence: (3) Here, the cost function C(a, b) quantifies the discrepancy between vectors a and b.
label: none

sentence: For instance, a common choice is the quadratic cost function C(a, b) = ||a −b||2 2.
label: none

sentence: It is to be emphasized that training typically refers to the task of determining θ, given training data, network architecture, and the cost function.
label: none

sentence: However, in practice, selecting training data (if not provided), defining network architecture, and choosing the cost function may also be viewed as integral parts of the training process. 4 Solving the optimization problem The optimization problem (3) is often solved by a gradient-based method, such as stochastic gradient descent [1, 2] or Adam [3].
label: none

sentence: These methods compute the gradient of the loss function with respect to the network parameters through the chain rule, using a differentiation technique known as backpropagation [4].
label: none

sentence: In this section, we will provide a concise overview of stochastic gradient descent and backpropagation.
label: none

sentence: For more comprehensive insights, we refer to [5]. 4.1 Gradient descent approach Gradient descent (GD), also known as steepest descent, is an iterative optimization method.
label: none

sentence: Given a fixed network architecture with unknown parameters θ and a data batch {(x(m), y(m))}n m=1 within the context of multivariate regression, GD aims to minimize the empirical risk function Rn(θ), given in (3), through an iterative process.
label: none

sentence: Starting with an initial guess θ(0) for the minimizer, GD consecutively updates θ(k), the set of parameters at iteration level k ≥0, moving in the negative direction of the gradient of the empirical risk at θ(k), θ(k+1) = θ(k) −η ∇θRn(θ(k)), k = 0, 1, 2, . . . .

sentence: Before discussing the derivation of backpropagation algorithm, we establish some notations. • M ℓ j,k: weight of the connection from neuron k in layer ℓ−1 to neuron j in layer ℓ • bℓ j: bias of neuron j in layer ℓ • zℓ j = Pnℓ−1 k=1 M ℓ j,k aℓ−1 k + bℓ j: input of neuron j in layer ℓ • aℓ j = σℓ(zℓ j): output of neuron j in layer ℓ • δℓ j := ∂Cm ∂zℓ j : sensitivity of the cost function Cm to changes in the j-th neuron in layer ℓ.

sentence: (6) A more efficient strategy is to replace GD with mini-batch stochastic GD (SGD), wherein a small subset of nb ≪n training data points, known as a mini-batch, is randomly selected from the entire dataset, and a gradient descent step is applied based on this mini-batch: 9 • Divide the set of n training data points into ⌊n/nb⌉mini-batches of size nb ≪n, where ⌊.⌉ means that we either take the floor or the ceil of the number depending on the number. • Loop over all mini-batches containing nb data points (note that the last batch may have fewer or larger number of points than nb); ◦For each training data point in the mini-batch, i.e. for m = 1, . . . , nb, call the backpropagation algorithm (BACKPRO) and compute {∇bℓCm, ∇MℓCm}L ℓ=0; ◦Approximate the gradients by taking the sample average of all nb gradients: ∇MℓRn(θ(k)) ≈1 nb nb X m=1 ∇MℓCm(θ(k)), ∇bℓRn(θ(k)) ≈1 nb nb X m=1 ∇bℓCm(θ(k)); ◦Update the weights and biases according to (6), using the approximate gradients.

label: none

sentence: However, polynomials may not be sufficiently versatile or complex to capture intricate patterns or model complex functions.
label: none

sentence: For the same reason, polynomial activation functions are also avoided.
label: none

sentence: Acti- vation functions further offer the capability to to limit and control a neuron’s output as required.
label: none

sentence: This aspect becomes particularly important in scenarios where the network output must adhere to specific constraints, such as being positive or bounded within a certain range, e.g., on [0,1].
label: none

sentence: In addition to the aforementioned features, activation functions should possess several desirable properties.
label: none

sentence: Firstly, since activation functions are applied multiple times, typically PL ℓ=0 nℓtimes in each forward pass, they should be computationally efficient to calculate, requiring only a few operations.
label: none

sentence: Secondly, they should be (almost everywhere) differentiable to facilitate the computation of (generalized) gradients of the loss function; refer to [6] for convergence analysis of gradient-based optimization methods, particularly in cases where activation functions are not differentiabile everywhere, such as Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) functions.
label: none

sentence: Moreover, activation functions should avoid the issue of vanishing gradients.
label: none

sentence: In the backpropagation algorithm, multiple applications of the chain rule occur.

sentence: For example, if σ′ ℓtakes values between 10 0 and 1 across many layers, or if σ′ ℓat a certain layer is close to zero (e.g., when σℓis flat), then δℓand consequently the gradient values at initial layers (with small ℓ) become very small.
label: none

sentence: Consequently, the weights and biases of these initial layers would learn slowly, leading to the vanishing gradient problem.
label: none

sentence: To mitigate this issue, it is preferable to use an activation function that avoids diminishing gradients, such as an increasing function whose derivative remains greater than or equal to 1 over a large part of its domain.

sentence: It transforms the network’s output into a set of pseudo-probabilities p1, . . . , pnL with PnL j=1 pj = 1.

sentence: ReLU stands out as one of the most favored activation functions in contemporary neural networks.
label: none

sentence: Its computational efficiency and avoidance of the vanishing gradient issue make it highly desirable.
label: none

sentence: ReLU’s (weak) derivative is 0 for negative inputs and 1 for non-negative ones, but it introduces a phenomenon known as dying ReLU.
label: none

sentence: This occurs when ReLU outputs zero for negative inputs, potentially causing some neurons to remain inactive.
label: none

sentence: Despite this, dying ReLU contributes to model sparsity, akin to the sparsity observed in biological neural networks: among billions of neurons in a human brain, only a portion of them fire (i.e. are active) at a time for a particular task.
label: none

sentence: Sparse networks offer advantages: they are more concise, less prone to overfitting, and faster to compute due to fewer operations.
label: none

sentence: The downside is the risk of some neurons becoming permanently inactive if they consistently receive negative inputs.
label: none

sentence: However, this scenario is less likely in practice, as SGD typically involves multiple data points, providing opportunities for non-negative inputs.

sentence: Leaky ReLU offers also a solution to the dying ReLU problem by introducing a small slope in the negative range.

label: none

sentence: The first step in avoiding overfitting is to detect overfitting.
label: none

sentence: For this purpose, we usually split the available data into two categories: training data and test data (or sometimes validation data).
label: none

sentence: While the network undergoes training using the training data, we monitor how the loss on this set evolves.
label: none

sentence: Simultaneously, we track the loss on the test data to gauge the network’s generalization ability.
label: none

sentence: A scenario depicted in Figure 2 illustrates a common observation: the loss on the training data decreases as the network learns, indicating a good fit to this dataset.
label: none

sentence: However, the loss on the test data initially decreases but later starts to rise.
label: none

sentence: This phenomenon signifies overfitting and suggests a lack of generalization.
label: none

sentence: Reducing overfitting can be achieved by increasing the amount of training data or by simplifying the network’s complexity, i.e., decreasing the number of network parameters.
label: none

sentence: However, these approaches are often impractical.
label: none

sentence: Augmenting the training dataset may not be feasible due to limitations in availability or cost.
label: none

sentence: Additionally, networks with a larger parameter count, such as deep networks, possess greater potential for power, making complexity reduction less desirable; we will discuss the power of “depth” in more details in the next chapters.
label: none

sentence: Fortunately, there are alternative strategies to mitigate overfitting within fixed constraints of data points and network parameters.
label: none

sentence: These include introducing regularization terms to the loss function, early stopping, and employing dropout. 12 Figure 2: The loss on training data versus test data as the number of epochs increases. 7.1 Adding penalty terms In this approach, we modify the loss function by adding a regularizing (or penalty) term.
label: none

sentence: Commonly used penalty terms include the L1-norm and L2-norm of all weights (parameters excluding biases), scaled by a factor λ.
label: none

sentence: This yields the regularized loss: Rn(θ) = 1 n n X m=1 Cm(θ) + λ ||θw||2.
label: none

sentence: Here, θw represents the vector of all weights excluding biases, and ||.|| denotes either the L1 or L2 norm.
label: none

sentence: The parameter λ > 0 serves as the regularization parameter, a hyper-parameter that requires tuning.
label: none

sentence: This type of regularization introduces a compromise between minimizing the original loss and reducing weights, with λ determining the balance.
label: none

sentence: Smaller weights, encouraged by regularization, result in more stable outputs with less sensitivity to small changes in input, akin to simpler models which are more generalizable.
label: none

sentence: With small weights, the network’s output would not change much if we make small changes in the input.
label: none

sentence: Additionally, regularization promotes convexity in the loss function, making optimization algorithms more robust against local minima and less dependent on the initial guess.
label: none

sentence: Biases are excluded from regularization because large biases do not significantly affect network sensitivity to input.
label: none

sentence: The difference between L1 and L2 regularization lies in how weights decrease during each iteration of GD/SGD.
label: none

sentence: For a single weight w := M ℓ j,k, the updates are as follows: • L1 regularization: w(k+1) = w(k) −η n Pn m=1 ∂Cm ∂w −η λ sgn(w(k)), • L2 regularization: w(k+1) = w(k) −η n Pn m=1 ∂Cm ∂w −2 η λ w(k).
label: none

sentence: In both cases, the penalty terms cause |w| to decrease.
label: none

sentence: However, L1 regularization decreases |w| by a fixed amount, whereas L2 regularization decreases |w| proportionally to |w|.
label: none

sentence: As a result, L2 regularization reduces large weights more than L1 regularization does, leading to a more balanced 13 weight distribution resembling a mean, while L1 regularization tends to keep some weights of high importance, akin to a median.
label: none

sentence: Moreover, L2 regularization maintains non-zero small weights, resulting in a dense weight vector, while L1 regularization induces sparsity by driving small weights to zero. 7.2 Early stopping In this approach, we divide the data into three sets: training, test, and validation.
label: none

sentence: The loss on the validation set is monitored at the end of each epoch.
label: none

sentence: Training stops when the validation loss no longer decreases, indicating that further training may lead to overfitting.
label: none

sentence: Refer to Section 8 for a more detailed utilization of the validation set. 7.3 Dropout In the dropout approach [7], we modify the network training process, rather than modifying the loss function.
label: none

sentence: During each mini-batch iteration, we randomly deactivate a portion of hidden neurons, e.g. half.
label: none

sentence: These deactivated neurons, along with their connections, are temporarily removed from the network.
label: none

sentence: Forward and backward passes are then performed on the modified network, updating weights and biases only for the active neurons.
label: none

sentence: This process is repeated for each mini-batch, with restoring the dropout neurons in the previous mini-batch and randomly selecting a new set of dropout neurons.
label: none

sentence: After training, dropout is no longer used during prediction.
label: none

sentence: Since the full network has twice as many active hidden neurons during training, the weights “outgoing” from these neurons are halved.
label: none

sentence: More generally, during training, each hidden neuron is retained with a fixed probability p, and during testing, the outgoing weights of each hidden neuron are scaled by p.
label: none

sentence: We note that to effectively remove a neuron from the network, its output weight is multiplied by zero.
label: none

sentence: Hence, only the output weights are scaled by the selected rate, while biases remain unchanged.
label: none

sentence: Conceptually, dropout simulates training numerous sparse neural networks in parallel, introducing regularization through the averaging of diverse model behaviors: different models may overfit in different ways, and hence averaging helps mitigate overfitting. 8 Validation and hyper-parameter tuning Every optimization/regularization technique involves hyper-parameters such as learning rates, number of epochs, mini-batch sizes, dropout rates, etc. These hyper-parameters are often opti- mized using a validation set, separate from the training data.
