sentence: Computationally efficient reductions between some statistical models Mengqi Lou⋆, Guy Bresler‡, Ashwin Pananjady⋆,† Schools of ⋆Industrial and Systems Engineering and †Electrical and Computer Engineering, Georgia Tech ‡Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, MIT September 19, 2024 Abstract We study the problem of approximately transforming a sample from a source statistical model to a sample from a target statistical model without knowing the parameters of the source model, and construct several computationally efficient such reductions between canonical statis- tical experiments.
label: none

sentence: In particular, we provide computationally efficient procedures that approx- imately reduce uniform, Erlang, and Laplace location models to general target families.
label: none

sentence: We illustrate our methodology by establishing nonasymptotic reductions between some canonical high-dimensional problems, spanning mixtures of experts, phase retrieval, and signal denoising.
label: none

sentence: Notably, the reductions are structure-preserving and can accommodate missing data.
label: none

sentence: We also point to a possible application in transforming one differentially private mechanism to another. 1 Introduction A statistical model or experiment is a collection of probability measures defined on a common sample space.
label: none

sentence: The notation (X, {Pθ}θ∈Θ) is typically used to denote a parametric statistical model on the sample space X, where θ is an unknown parameter and Pθ is the corresponding probability model from which a random sample of observations is drawn.
label: none

sentence: The following classical question, first asked by Bohnenblust et al. (1949), forms the starting point of this paper: When is one statistical experiment more informative than another?
label: none

sentence: (Q1) The question can be reframed colloquially for two parametric statistical models given by U = (X, {Pθ}θ∈Θ) (the source) and V = (Y, {Qθ}θ∈Θ) (the target), defined on possibly different sample spaces X and Y, respectively.
label: none

sentence: For every θ ∈Θ and without knowledge of θ, can a sample from the source distribution Pθ be transformed into a sample from the distribution Qθ?
label: none

sentence: In other words, does there exist some randomized procedure K (a reduction) such that for every value of θ ∈Θ, if X ∼Pθ, then the random variable K(X) has the distribution Qθ.
label: none

sentence: If so, the problem of recovering the unknown parameter θ from a sample of the source statistical model U can now be solved by a recovery procedure that uses a sample from the target statistical model V.
label: none

sentence: The concept was further built on by Blackwell in a series of papers (Blackwell, 1951, 1953), where he formalized so-called comparison criteria between experiments in the context of the min- imum risk attainable by statistical procedures.
label: none

sentence: There followed a beautiful line of follow-up work (see, e.g., Boll (1955); Lindley (1956); Strassen (1965); Hansen and Torgersen (1974) and Le Cam (1996) for a survey).
label: none

sentence: Somewhat unfortunately, however, it was found that most experiments were incomparable (see, e.g., Stone (1961) for some examples).
label: research_gap

sentence: In fact, very few exact comparisons between experiments are known—and all explicit examples of such exact reductions (amounting to 1 arXiv:2402.07717v2 [math.ST] 18 Sep 2024 less than five families of procedures) can be found in the books by Torgersen (1991) and Shiryaev and Spokoiny (2000).
label: research_gap

sentence: Accordingly, various approximate notions of comparisons between experiments were introduced (e.g. Karlin and Rubin (1956); Brown et al. (1976); Goel and DeGroot (1979); Lehmann (1988)).
label: none

sentence: The most popular among these is the notion of approximate sufficiency formalized by the total variation deficiency between experiments (Le Cam, 1964).
label: none

sentence: Instead of asking when one could exactly reduce the source experiment to the target, Le Cam asked a relaxations of this question, asking when one could produce an inexact reduction that is accurate up to some total variation distance.
label: none

sentence: In other words, he was interested in a reduction attaining small total variation deficiency, thereby relaxing the above question (Q1) to: How far is one statistical experiment from another?
label: none

sentence: (Q2) Equivalently, what is the smallest value δ so that there exists a randomized procedure K (an approximate reduction) with the property that for all θ ∈Θ, if X ∼Pθ, then the distribution of K(X) is δ-close in total variation to Qθ?
label: none

sentence: Similarly to its exact analog, an approximate reduction allows us to transfer procedures and risk guarantees from the source to taget model (see Eq. (4) to follow).
label: none

sentence: Le Cam then used the notion of deficiency to define a distance between experiments, which has come to be known as the Le Cam distance.
label: none

sentence: Note that the question (Q2)—as with the original question (Q1) of exact comparisons—remains reasonable for any pair of statistical experiments, even those with a single observation.
label: none

sentence: A specific form of this question forms the focus of the present paper, since it is an important consideration in high dimensions.
label: none

sentence: To see this more clearly in an example, consider the problem of producing approximate re- ductions between experiments when there is a high-dimensional parameter and independent noise across coordinates.
label: none

sentence: A prototypical example is the structured mean estimation problem, where Θ ⊆Rn is some structured set, and we obtain a single noisy observation of a vector θ ∈Θ from the source model Pθ = P1 θ1 × · · · Pn θn, where θk denotes the k-th entry of θ and the noisy obser- vations are independent across coordinates given the parameter.
label: none

sentence: Other isomorphic examples are those in which the parameter set is a class of matrices or tensors.
label: none

sentence: Now suppose we are interested in reducing our observation to some target model Qθ = Q1 θ1 × · · · Qn θn, effectively changing the noise distribution while preserving the underlying parameter.
label: none

sentence: Then one conceptually robust way to do so is to produce entry-by-entry approximate reductions that are agnostic to the structure in the set Θ, i.e., to approximately reduce source Pk θk to target Qk θk for each k = 1, . . . , n, thereby producing n scalar approximate reductions.
label: none

sentence: An important feature of this problem that is worth emphasizing is that, owing to the high-dimensional setting, we obtain just a single observation per coordinate, and so our reduction1 must be accurate in a regime where the parameter itself cannot be accurately estimated.
label: none

sentence: While single-sample reductions of the above flavor were the original focus of classical papers (e.g. Hansen and Torgersen (1974); Lehmann (1988)), they have seen renewed interest in the con- text of high-dimensional problems in statistics and applied probability, especially for transferring average-case computational hardness of estimation and testing tasks so as to provide lower bounds on the (computationally) constrained minimax risk (Berthet and Rigollet, 2013; Wainwright, 2014; Brennan and Bresler, 2020; Wu and Xu, 2021).
label: none

sentence: The idea of transferring computational hardness via reduction has been foundational in theoretical computer science since the start of the field, and in our setting goes as follows: Suppose we believe that estimating θ from the statistical model U is computationally difficult (in that a computationally efficient algorithm does not exist), and also that we have a computationally efficient, approximate reduction from the source U to target V that 1In the sequel, we will largely deal with approximate reductions, but refer to these as reductions for convenience. 2 attains arbitrarily small total variation (TV) deficiency.
label: none

sentence: Then estimating θ from the statistical model V must also be difficult.
label: none

sentence: To see this, suppose for the sake of contradiction that we indeed have a computationally efficient estimation algorithm in the statistical model V = (Y, {Qθ}θ∈Θ).
label: none

sentence: Then we could perform estimation in U = (X, {Pθ}θ∈Θ) by drawing our source sample, performing the reduction, and using our estimation algorithm for V = (Y, {Qθ}θ∈Θ) to recover θ.
label: none

sentence: Note that this yields a computationally efficient procedure for estimating θ using the source experiment U, which is a contradiction.
label: none

sentence: Similar ideas apply to the testing problem.
label: none

sentence: A key desideratum that these reductions must satisfy—in addition to the TV closeness property alluded to above—is that they must be implementable in a computationally efficient manner.
label: none

sentence: This property distinguishes this line of work from (Q2) above.
label: none

sentence: Indeed, there exists source/target experiments such that their Le Cam distance is small but the reduction procedure cannot be computed in polynomial time under natural conjectures in average-case complexity.
label: none

sentence: We provide such an example in Appendix A.
label: none

sentence: With this setup in place, let us now discuss a few lines of related work to provide context, followed by our contributions. 1.1 Related work We split our discussion of related work into a few verticals.
label: none

sentence: Single-sample reductions: With the motivation sketched above, Hajek et al. (2015); Ma and Wu (2015) provided computationally efficient reductions from “two-point” source experiments— where both X and Θ are sets containing two discrete values—to a family of target experiments having two distinct means.
label: none

sentence: Both papers took the approach of entry-by-entry, single-sample re- ductions to transforming the planted clique model, which is believed to be computationally hard from an average-case complexity standpoint, to variants of the planted submatrix detection prob- lem.
label: none

sentence: Specifically, Hajek et al. (2015) provided a single-sample reduction from a pair of Bernoulli models with different means to a pair of Binomial models with different means, and Ma and Wu (2015) gave a single-sample reduction from a pair of Bernoulli models with different means to a pair of unit-variance Gaussian models with different means.
label: none

sentence: Following up on this work, Brennan et al. (2018) gave generalizations of these reductions to univariate target distributions along with a number of other results.
label: none

sentence: Brennan et al. (2019) also considered two-point sources and general, multivariate target distributions, showing a universality property for computational hardness in submatrix detection problems.
label: none

sentence: Subsequently, (Brennan and Bresler, 2020) demonstrated a univer- sality result for estimation in sparse mixture problems by devising a reduction from three-point source distributions—where both X and Θ are sets containing three discrete values.
label: none

sentence: The aforementioned reductions between statistical models have been used as ingredients— sometimes alongside modified conjectures in average-case complexity and careful transformations of structure between problem instances (Brennan and Bresler, 2020)—to show computational hard- ness for a host of high-dimensional statistical problems with combinatorial structure, including (but not limited to) principal component analysis with structure (e.g., Brennan and Bresler, 2019; Wang et al., 2023), location and mixture models with adversarial corruptions (Brennan and Bresler, 2020), block models in both matrix (Brennan et al., 2018) and tensor (e.g., Luo and Zhang, 2022; Han et al., 2022) settings, tensor PCA (Brennan and Bresler, 2020), and adaptation lower bounds in shape-constrained regression problems (e.g., Pananjady and Samworth, 2022).
label: none

sentence: However, the reduc- tions between statistical models are limited to those with either two or three unknown parameters.
label: research_gap

sentence: In this paper, we will handle several cases where the parameter set is continuous. 3 Asymptotic perspectives: A complementary literature to the non-asymptotic perspective sketched above—with several classical results—is one that views this problem through an asymptotic lens.
label: none

sentence: Indeed, after asking question (Q2) above, Le Cam considered asymptotic convergence, in his Le Cam distance, of a sequence of experiments indexed by the size of an i.i.d. sample.
label: none

sentence: He asked if such a sequence converges to a limit, and in a set of landmark results, showed that under some reg- ularity conditions and with appropriate rescaling, one has convergence to a Gaussian experiment, i.e., a remarkable strengthening of the central limit theorem.
label: none

sentence: This result was a cornerstone for the theory of local asymptotic normality, which along with its counterpart theory of local asymptotic minimaxity has resulted in several groundbreaking discoveries in mathematical statistics over the years; see Le Cam and Yang (2000); van der Vaart (2000) for a more thorough exposition.
label: none

sentence: Notably, Le Cam’s asymptotic theory has an analog for nonparametric models2, as was proved in a line of influential work relating nonparametric regression in the white noise and fixed design models, as well as nonparametric density estimation (Nussbaum, 1996; Brown and Low, 1996; Brown et al., 2002; Carter, 2002; Brown et al., 2004).
label: none

sentence: In the context of the present paper, it is important to note that this line of work has a com- plementary focus and is not applicable to the structured high-dimensional settings that motivate our work.
label: research_gap

sentence: First, asymptotic equivalence of experiments has been used mainly in the analysis of natural estimators—for example, to show that the MLE in a quadratic mean differentiable model is asymptotically Gaussian (van der Vaart, 2000).
label: none

sentence: Second, and on a related note, the reductions inherently rely on large sample sizes and some form of convergence in distribution guaranteed by the central limit theorem.
label: none

sentence: In particular, they only succeed in regimes where the parameter itself is estimable from the data, and so the reductions used in these techniques typically do not perform any sophisticated processing of the source sample, even in complex models (Shiryaev and Spokoiny, 2000).
label: research_gap

sentence: Consequently, while they are useful for analytical purposes, these reductions do not provide a path to characterizing the deficiency between general statistical models (as framed in question (Q2)) when we have a single (or fixed-size) observation, which, as alluded to before, is the key issue in high-dimensional problems.
label: research_gap

sentence: Other related papers: Besides these two lines of literature dealing explictly with reductions, we also mention some related investigations.
label: none

sentence: See Huber (1965) for a classical two-point reduction inspired by robust hypothesis testing.
label: none

sentence: The theory of channel comparisons is a related concept, and has seen a line of important work (Shannon, 1958; Raginsky, 2011; Polyanskiy and Wu, 2017; Makur and Polyanskiy, 2018); see Polyanskiy and Wu (2023+) for an introduction.
label: none

sentence: The problem of approximate reductions between statistical models is also related to the recently introduced concept of simultaneous optimal transport (Wang and Zhang, 2022). 1.2 Contributions, motivating examples, and organization In this paper, we revisit the problem of constructing non-asymptotic, computationally efficient, approximate reductions between families of source and target statistical models.
label: none

sentence: In doing so, we consider source distributions with continuous parameter spaces, going well beyond the two and three-point cases considered in prior work.
label: none

sentence: In particular, we introduce two general-purpose techniques to construct these reductions, and showcase them by giving explicit reductions between Laplace, Erlang, and Uniform location models and general families of target models, all of which are new.
label: none

sentence: In the process, we show some exact reductions (in the sense of Blackwell (1951)) that, to our knowledge, had not been pointed out in the literature. 2See Mariucci (2016) for a modern survey of this literature. 4 Our techniques demonstrate that it is possible to achieve non-asymptotic approximate reduc- tions for several natural statistical models with continuous parameters.
label: none

sentence: These can in turn show near-equivalence results for several problems in high-dimensional statistics.
label: none

sentence: As motivation, we next give some examples of high-dimensional problems for which a formal reduction algorithm would be meaningful.
label: none

sentence: These examples serve as an informal preview: They are formally presented again in Section 5 along with explicit guarantees that result from our general theory.
label: none

sentence: Motivation 1 The mixture of experts model has been influential in studying heterogeneous regression problems with so-called “gating” functions.
label: none

sentence: In a canonical version of the model, the scalar response Y ∈R and high-dimensional covariates X ∈Rd are related via the model E[Y |X] = sign(g(X))·f(X) for some unknown regression function f ∈F and gating function g ∈G.
label: none

sentence: Variants of this model have been extensively studied under several, often parametric, assumptions on the noise (e.g., Jordan and Jacobs, 1994; Song et al., 2014).
label: none

sentence: A related model is one of signless regression, in which we have E[Y |X] = |f(X)|, which has also been studied under various models for the regression function and noise process (e.g., Cai et al., 2016; Duchi and Ruan, 2019).
label: none

sentence: When F is the class of linear functions, the two statistical models go by the names of “mixture of linear regressions” and “phase retrieval”, respectively.
label: none

sentence: Given the similarity between the models, it is natural to ask: Is there a reduction that would allow us to solve a noisy mixture of experts problem through a phase retrieval algorithm when the dimension d is large?
label: none

sentence: Motivation 2 In signal denoising problems of the form Y = θ∗+ ϵ, we often have sharp charac- terizations of the error of estimators when the noise ϵ is Gaussian.
label: none

sentence: For example, if the signal θ∗is known to belong to a closed convex set in Rn, we can exactly characterize (with both upper and lower bounds that match up to a universal constant) the ℓ2 risk of the least squares estimator under zero-mean Gaussian noise (Chatterjee, 2014).
label: none

sentence: While upper bounds of this type can sometimes be proved for other noise distributions (e.g., when ϵ is drawn from a zero-mean sub-Gaussian), it is not clear if such bounds are sharp in the same way.
label: research_gap

sentence: With the goal of producing an estimator with sharp error guarantees, can we design a reduction from a given statistical model of interest—where θ∗is known to obey some structure and the noise is known to be drawn from some distribution (e.g., Sambasivan and Haupt, 2018; McRae and Davenport, 2021)—to one that is arbitrarily close to a Gaussian model?
label: none

sentence: Can we do so in natural settings with structured signals and missing data?
label: none

sentence: Motivation 3 There are several privacy-preserving mechanisms for data analysis, and many rely on the notion of differential privacy, which is often guaranteed by adding noise from a certain dis- tribution to the output of a database query (Dwork, 2006).
label: none

sentence: Several such noise addition mechanisms have been proposed and studied in the literature, and each comes with its own set of operational advantages.
label: none

sentence: A natural question is whether one can transform between these mechanisms in a down- stream fashion, that is, without needing to de-privatize the query itself.
label: none

sentence: For two popular privacy preserving mechanisms, this natural question is equivalent to one covered by our setting: Can a Laplace random variable (or vector) of unknown mean can be transformed into a Gaussian random variable (or vector) of the same mean?
label: none

sentence: How does the resulting mechanism compare with a direct Gaussian mechanism in terms of its privacy and accuracy guarantee?
label: none

sentence: The rest of this paper is organized as follows.
label: none

sentence: In Section 2, we formally present the problem of constructing reductions with minimal total variation deficiency, and discuss why a natural reduction may be a poor candidate for this problem.
label: none

sentence: In Section 3, we make the oracle assumption that we are given some candidate “signed kernel” between the source and target experiments, and provide a computationally efficient algorithm for generating a sample that resembles one from the target 5 experiment.
label: none

sentence: In Section 4, we use this result alongside explicit constructions of signed kernels for source models given by the multivariate Laplace and univariate Erlang and Uniform location models, and provide explicit reductions for general target models.
label: none

sentence: We present applications to high- dimensional problems in Section 5, including answers to the questions posed in Motivations 1-3 above.
label: none

sentence: We conclude with a discussion of open problems in Section 6.

sentence: To make things concrete, consider a database of n individuals given by (X1, . . . , Xn) ∈X n and a function f : X n →R that we wish to compute in a differentially private fashion via a (possibly randomized) mechanism g : X n →R.

label: none

sentence: The mechanism g is said to be (ϵ, δ) differentially private if for all Borel sets B ⊆R and neighboring databases (X, Y ), we have P(g(X) ∈B) ≤exp(ϵ) · P(g(Y ) ∈B) + δ.
label: none

sentence: An important consideration is how f itself behaves on neighboring databases.
label: none

sentence: The sensitivity of f is given by ϕ(f) = max X,Y neighbors |f(X) −f(Y )|.
label: none

sentence: While any query can be made private with the addition of enough noise, one also desires that the mechanism be useful, in that the output of the mechanism is close to the desired query.

sentence: If we wanted to now produce a Gaussian mechanism (in the classical sense), then we would need to recover the original ERM solution—which in turn requires re-solving the ERM problem and de-privatization— and corrupt it with Gaussian noise.
label: none

sentence: In contrast, one might be interested in a direct approach that uses the output of the already executed Laplace mechanism.
label: none

sentence: Does such a transformation exist?
label: none

sentence: An application of Theorem 1 answers this question in the affirmative.

sentence: Suppose g is given by the Laplace mechanism in Proposition 6, and let Z ∼N(0, 2b2 log(12/δ)) denote a Gaussian random variable drawn independently of everything else.

sentence: For each X ∈X n, there is a mechanism h constructible in time polynomial in 1/δ purely from g(X) (without access to f or X) such that dTV(h, f(X) + Z) ≤δ. 25 In particular, the mechanism h is  ϕ(f) b , 0  differentially private for f with accuracy r 2b2 log(12/δ) + 2b2 + b2 4 · δ log3/2(12/δ).

sentence: Corollary 3 is proved in Section 7.12.

sentence: A few comments are in order.
label: none

sentence: First, note that the created mechanism h is a postprocessing of the Laplace mechanism, and hence inherits its differential privacy guarantee (see Dwork and Roth (2014, Theorem 3.14)).
label: none

sentence: Second, it achieves nearly the same privacy-accuracy tradeoff that is achieved by the classical Gaussian mechanism, which has access to f(X) and corrupts this query output with Gaussian noise having the same variance as Z in Corollary 3 (see Dwork and Roth (2014, Appendix A)).
label: none

sentence: The similarity of the two privacy- accuracy tradeoffs is particularly clear when δ ↓0, where the accuracy guarantee of h tends to the limit p 2b2 log(12/δ), which is precisely the standard deviation of the Gaussian Z.
label: none

sentence: In other words, adding Laplace noise to privatize data gives, to a degree, a universal mechanism, in that the result of this mechanism can be transformed, downstream, to resemble an “oracle” Gaussian mechanism that is created with access to f.
label: none

sentence: Third, note that Corollary 3 provides an alternative proof that the classical Gaussian mechanism f(X) + Z is  ϕ(f) b , δ  differentially private.
label: none

sentence: Such a proof is illuminating because it explicitly exhibits a  ϕ(f) b , 0  mechanism—one that can be realized via post- processing of the Laplace mechanism—that is δ-close in total variation to the Gaussian mechanism.
label: none

sentence: This provides a construction of an intermediate mechanism that witnesses the conditions in Dwork and Roth (2014, Lemma 3.17), which state (roughly speaking) that for any (ϵ, δ) mechanism M, there must exist an (ϵ, 0) mechanism that is δ close to M in total variation.
label: none

sentence: Note that our main lemma (Lemma 1) is not limited to these reductions, and can in principle be applied much more broadly.

sentence: As concrete consequences, we covered prob- lems spanning mixture modeling, denoising, missing data, and privacy.

sentence: As alluded to in Sections 2 and 5, we expect our results to have several consequences not covered here, specifically to proving (computationally constrained) minimax lower bounds.
label: future_work

sentence: Our work leaves open several questions; let us list a few here.
label: future_work

sentence: First, note that as articulated in Remarks 3 and 4, the differentiability properties of source and target appear crucial to pro- ducing good reductions via the techniques introduced in this paper.
label: none

sentence: In particular, all the source distributions that we have considered have nondifferentiable densities, and the corresponding target densities are at least as smooth as the respective source distributions.
label: limitation

sentence: In particular, a reduction from a very smooth source density (such as a Gaussian) appears to be out of the reach of our tech- niques, unless the target is also Gaussian.
label: limitation

sentence: It is an interesting open problem to prove a nontrivial reduction from a Gaussian source model, since it would be particular useful in transferring lower bounds from the canonical Gaussian location model to other noise models.
label: future_work

sentence: The second set of questions pertains to our construction of a Markov kernel.
label: none

sentence: Indeed, Algo- rithm rk was designed to sample from the Markov kernel bT (8), which was, in turn, a simple thresholded version of our oracle signed kernel.
label: none

sentence: Is such a construction optimal given access to a 26 signed kernel S∗satisfying ς(U, V; S∗) = 0?
label: future_work

sentence: Can we directly pursue the optimal Markov kernel by approximately solving the infinite-dimensional linear program (1b) for some interesting class of source and target families?
label: future_work

sentence: A third direction would be to extend approximate reductions beyond total variation deficiency.
label: future_work

sentence: Indeed, it is reasonable to define notions of deficiency—i.e., ask question (Q2)—in any “distance” between probability measures, with natural choices being the family of f-divergences, R´enyi diver- gences, and integral probability metrics.
label: none

sentence: What forms do corresponding reductions take, and are they significantly different from reductions in total variation?

sentence: How does the choice of divergence influence the particular data processing inequality that must be satisfied in order to map source to target?
label: future_work

sentence: As a final direction, we reiterate that an important application of reductions between experi- ments is to transfer risk bounds and algorithmic lower bounds, and we pose a few concrete questions in this vein.
label: future_work

sentence: The paradigm of smoothed analysis (Spielman and Teng, 2004) has been extensively applied to explain the practical efficiency of algorithms that are inefficient in the worst-case.
label: none

sentence: More generally, average-case analysis of algorithms provides a framework to reason about the properties of algorithms when run on random instances of problems.
label: none

sentence: These definitions rely intrinsically on the perturbations of an instance by noise that is chosen from a particular distribution, and this distri- bution is in turn chosen in some ad-hoc fashion.
label: research_gap

sentence: Reductions between problem instances corrupted by different noise distributions would show that similar insights hold for several other perturbation distributions.
label: future_work

sentence: A distinct application is to prove lower bounds on particular classes of algorithms (or models of computation) for high-dimensional statistics problems, and not all computationally efficient algorithms as alluded to in Section 2.
label: future_work

sentence: Examples include algorithms that utilize low-degree polynomials of data (Hopkins, 2018; Kunisky et al., 2019) or the sum-of-squares hierarchy (Barak et al., 2019).
label: none

sentence: If the reduction between source and target can be performed by an algorithm that is itself implementable by a certain model of computation, then it would show that lower bounds on this model of computation transfer from source to target instances.
label: future_work

sentence: LXMERT Model Compression for Visual Question Answering Maryam Hashemi Ghazaleh Mahmoudi ∗ Sara Kodeiri∗ Hadi Sheikhi∗Sauleh Eetemadi School of Computer Engineering, Iran University of Science and Technology, Iran {m hashemi94, gh mahmoodi, sara kodeiri, ha sheikhi}@comp.iust.ac.ir, sauleh@iust.ac.ir Abstract Large-scale pretrained models such as LXMERT are becoming popular for learning cross-modal representations on text-image pairs for vision-language tasks.
label: none

sentence: According to the lottery ticket hypothesis, NLP and computer vision models contain smaller subnetworks capable of being trained in isolation to full performance.
label: none

sentence: In this paper, we combine these observations to evaluate whether such trainable subnetworks exist in LXMERT when fine-tuned on the VQA task.
label: none

sentence: In addition, we perform a model size cost-benefit analysis by investigating how much pruning can be done without significant loss in accuracy.
label: none

sentence: Our experiment results demonstrate that LXMERT can be effectively pruned by 40%-60% in size with 3% loss in accuracy. 1 Introduction and Related Work Over the past few years, many single-modal pre- trained models have been proposed.
label: none

sentence: Inspired by this, the vision-and-language pretraining seeks to learn joint representations using visual and tex- tual content to improve the efficiency of vision- language tasks.
label: none

sentence: Both single-modality and cross-modality pre- trained models often have hundreds of millions of parameters.
label: none

sentence: Unfortunately, training these over- parametrized models can be prohibitively time- consuming and costly, making them impractical for resource-limited devices.
label: research_gap

sentence: However, cross-modality pretrained models suffer more from the increased model size due to the higher input space dimension.
label: research_gap

sentence: With the task of Visual Question Answering (VQA) (Antol et al., 2015) in mind, and its ultimate goal of being helpful to the visually impaired, decreasing V+L model size makes it feasible to use them in limited-resource devices.
label: none

sentence: To address this problem, model compression techniques such as pruning have been developed. ∗These authors contributed equally.
label: none

sentence: Deep Learning recently enjoyed welcoming a new powerful pruning method: The Lottery Ticket Hy- pothesis (LTH) (Frankle and Carbin, 2019).
label: none

sentence: LTH has been shown great success in various fields.
label: none

sentence: It could be a powerful tool to understand the parame- ter redundancy in the current pretrained V+L mod- els.
label: none

sentence: Thus, we aim to apply LTH to LXMERT(Tan and Bansal, 2020), one of the best-performing two- stream V+L models, to fill this gap.
label: none

sentence: We evaluate our work on VQA (Antol et al., 2015) and com- pare it with DistillVLM(Fang et al., 2021), which leverages the knowledge distillation technique to compress large visual-linguistic models.
label: none

sentence: Similar to this work, Gan et al. (2021) study LTH for UNITER(Chen et al., 2020).
label: none

sentence: However, UNITER is a single stream V+L model, and LXMERT is a two-stream model; our results are consistent with theirs. 2 Methodology In this section, we briefly explain the LXMERT ar- chitecture and LTH.
label: none

sentence: Then, we describe how we use LTH to compress the pretrained LXMERT model.
label: none

sentence: LXMERT is a Transformer-based model which takes two inputs: image and text.
label: none

sentence: Internally, LXMERT consists of two types of encoders: single- modality encoders for each modality and a cross- modality encoder using bidirectional cross atten- tion to exchange information and align entities across the modalities.
label: none

sentence: The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (Frankle and Carbin, 2019) shows that by preserving the original weight initializations from the unpruned network, you can train a network with the topology of the pruned network and achieve the same or better test accuracy within the same number of training itera- tions.
label: none

sentence: In order to apply LTH to the LXMERT model, we use iterative magnitude pruning.
label: none

sentence: Therefore, we fine-tune LXMERT on the VQA task and itera- tively prune 10% of the lowest magnitude weights across the entire model, excluding embedding and arXiv:2310.15325v1 [cs.CV] 23 Oct 2023 Method test-dev test-std Yes/No Number other Overall Yes/No Number other Overall DistillVLM - - - 69.6 - - - 69.8 LXMERT 88.24 54.45 63.05 72.45 88.29 54.37 63.18 72.63 LXMERT (low-magnitude) 86.95 ± 0.95 52.60 ± 1.87 60.96 ± 1.76 70.72 ± 1.44 87.07 ± 1.12 52.28 ± 1.66 61.02 ± 1.83 70.87 ± 1.51 LXMERT (high-magnitude) 74.11 ± 0.91 42.81 ± 1.36 50.5 ± 0.19 59.35 ± 0.61 74.23 ± 0.81 42.99 ± 0.87 50.71 ± 0.26 59.62 ± 0.55 LXMERT (random) 69.26 ± 0.29 39.84 ± 0.93 45.96 ± 0.83 54.86 ± 0.52 69.27 ± 0.18 40.34 ± 0.66 46.33 ± 0.79 55.19 ± 0.45 Table 1: Performance of subnetworks at 50% weights pruning on VQA v2, which reported for both test-dev and test-std.

sentence: We use the default settings and hyperparameters of LXMERT (Tan and Bansal, 2020) to finetune on the VQA v2.0 dataset. 3 Experimental Setups and Results The experiments are designed to investigate the effectiveness and stability of LTH on LXMERT in addition to cost-benefit analysis of the number of parameters in the model.
label: none

sentence: We conduct experiments on the widely-used VQA v2.0 (Goyal et al., 2017) dataset built based on the MS-COCO (Lin et al., 2014) image corpus. 3.1 Effectiveness and Stability The following steps are performed to compress the LXMERT model. 1.
label: none

sentence: The pretrained LXMERT model plus the VQA classifier’s randomly initialized weights are saved. 2.
label: none

sentence: The model is fine-tuned on the 3,129 most frequent answers in the VQA v2.0 dataset. 3.
label: none

sentence: Iterative magnitude pruning is applied to find the low-magnitude subnetwork (pruning 50% of the low-magnitude weights).
label: none

sentence: The high- magnitude subnetwork is computed as a com- pliment of the low-magnitude subnetwork with equal size.
label: none

sentence: A random subnetwork with an equal size is generated for comparison. 4.
label: none

sentence: The saved weights are restored for all three subnetworks. 5.
label: none

sentence: The high-magnitude, low-magnitude, and ran- dom subnetworks are fine-tuned and evaluated on the VQA Task using three different seeds for initializing the VQA model to ensure the stability of the results.
label: none

sentence: Results of subnetworks at 50% weights prun- ing on VQA v2.0 are summarized in Table 1 where DistillVLM (Fang et al., 2021) is also listed for comparison.
label: none

sentence: Row 2 to row 5 reports respec- tively full finetuned LXMERT, low-magnitude, high-magnitude, and random subnetworks.
label: none

sentence: Low- magnitude pruning achieves 97% of full finetuned LXMERT accuracy in overall for both test-dev and test-std and shows marginal improvement over Dis- tillVLM as the baseline.
label: none

sentence: By comparing perfor- mance across the subnetworks, random and high magnitude subnetworks perform far worse than low-magnitude subnetwork.
label: none

sentence: Surprisingly, the re- sults demonstrate high-magnitude subnetwork per- forming better than random subnetwork.
label: none

sentence: This could be a LXMERT specific phenomenon and required further investigation. 3.2 Cost-Benefit Analysis We experiment with low-magnitude subnetwork by pruning 10% of the weights all the way up to 90% of the weights in 10% increments.
label: future_work

sentence: Accuracy of these pruned models on VQA v2.0 are reported in Figure 1.
label: none

sentence: Our results indicate a significant loss of accuracy after 50% to 60% pruning.
label: none

sentence: Figure 1: Model size cost-benefit analysis. 4 Conclusion We confirm that LTH pruning is an effective method for pruning V+L pretrained models.
label: none

sentence: We mainly focused on LXMERT, a two-stream V+L pretrained model, but our findings are consis- tent with Gan et al. (2021)’s results while using UNITER, a single-stream V+L pretrained model.
label: limitation

sentence: Speedy Performance Estimation for Neural Architecture Search Binxin Ru ∗ Department of Engineering Science University of Oxford robin@robots.ox.ac.uk Clare Lyle ∗ Department of Computer Science University of Oxford clare.lyle@univ.ox.ac.uk Lisa Schut Department of Computer Science University of Oxford lisa.schut@cs.ox.ac.uk Miroslav Fil Department of Computer Science University of Oxford miroslav.fil@seh.ox.ac.uk Mark van der Wilk Department of Computing Imperial College London m.vdwilk@imperial.ac.uk Yarin Gal Department of Computer Science University of Oxford yarin@cs.ox.ac.uk Abstract Reliable yet efﬁcient evaluation of generalisation performance of a proposed archi- tecture is crucial to the success of neural architecture search (NAS).
label: none

sentence: Traditional approaches face a variety of limitations: training each architecture to completion is prohibitively expensive, early stopped validation accuracy may correlate poorly with fully trained performance, and model-based estimators require large train- ing sets.
label: research_gap

sentence: We instead propose to estimate the ﬁnal test performance based on a simple measure of training speed.
label: none

sentence: Our estimator is theoretically motivated by the connection between generalisation and training speed, and is also inspired by the reformulation of a PAC-Bayes bound under the Bayesian setting.
label: none

sentence: Our model- free estimator is simple, efﬁcient, and cheap to implement, and does not require hyperparameter-tuning or surrogate training before deployment.
label: none

sentence: We demonstrate on various NAS search spaces that our estimator consistently outperforms other alternatives in achieving better correlation with the true test performance rankings.
label: none

sentence: We further show that our estimator can be easily incorporated into both query-based and one-shot NAS methods to improve the speed or quality of the search. 1 Introduction Reliably estimating the generalisation performance of a proposed architecture is crucial to the success of Neural Architecture Search (NAS) but has always been a major bottleneck in NAS algorithms [12].
label: research_gap

sentence: The traditional approach of training each architecture for a large number of epochs and evaluating it on validation data (full training) provides a reliable performance measure, but requires prohibitively large computational resources on the order of thousands of GPU days [52, 35, 53, 34, 12].
label: none

sentence: This motivates the development of methods for speeding up performance estimation to make NAS practical for limited computing budgets. ∗These authors contributed equally.
label: none

sentence: Under review. arXiv:2006.04492v2 [stat.ML] 8 Jun 2021 A popular simple approach is early-stopping, which offers a low-ﬁdelity approximation of general- isation performance by training for fewer epochs [23, 13, 21].
label: none

sentence: However, if we stop training early and evaluate the model on validation data, the relative performance ranking may not correlate well with the performance ranking of the full training [49], i.e. the test performance of the model after the entire trainin budget has been used.
label: research_gap

sentence: Another line of work focuses on learning curve extrapolation [10, 19, 3], which trains a surrogate model to predict the ﬁnal generalisation performance based on the initial learning curve and/or meta-features of the architecture.
label: none

sentence: However, the training of the surrogate often requires hundreds of fully evaluated architectures to achieve satisfactory extrapolation performance and the hyper-parameters of the surrogate also need to be optimised.
label: research_gap

sentence: Alternatively, the idea of weight sharing is adopted in one-shot NAS methods to speed up evaluation [32, 24, 43].
label: none

sentence: Despite leading to signiﬁcant cost-saving, weight sharing heavily underestimates the true performance of good architectures and is unreliable in predicting the relative ranking among architectures [45, 48].
label: research_gap

sentence: A more recent group of estimators claim to be zero-cost [27, 1].
label: none

sentence: Yet, their performance is often not competitive with the state of the art, inconsistent across tasks and cannot be further improved with additional training budgets.
label: research_gap

sentence: In view of the above limitations, we propose a simple model-free method, Training Speed Estimation (TSE), which provides a reliable yet computationally cheap estimate of the generalisation performance ranking of architectures.
label: none

sentence: Our method is inspired by recent empirical and theoretical results linking training speed and generalisation [16, 26] and measures the training speed of an architecture by summing the training losses of the commonly-used SGD optimiser during training.
label: none

sentence: We empirically show that our estimator can outperform strong existing approaches to predict the relative performance ranking among architectures, and can remain effective for a variety of search spaces and datasets.
label: none

sentence: Moreover, we verify its usefulness under different NAS settings and ﬁnd it can speed up query-based NAS approaches signiﬁcantly as well improve the performance of one-shot and differentiable NAS. 2 Method Motivation The theoretical relationship between training speed and generalisation is described in a number of existing works.
label: none

sentence: Stability-based generalisation bounds for SGD [16, 25] bound the generalisation gap of a model based on the number of optimisation steps used to train it.
label: none

sentence: These bounds predict that models which train faster obtain a lower worst-case generalisation error.
label: none

sentence: In networks of sufﬁcient width, a neural-tangent-kernel-inspired complexity measure can bound both the worst-case generalisation gap and the rate of convergence of (full-batch) gradient descent [2, 6].
label: none

sentence: However, these bounds cannot distinguish between models that are trained for the same number of steps but attain near-zero loss at different rates as they ignore the training trajectory.
label: research_gap

sentence: We instead draw inspiration from another approach which incorporates properties of the trajectory taken during SGD, seen in the information-theoretic generalisation bounds of [29] and [30].
label: none

sentence: These bounds depend on the variance of gradients computed during training, a quantity which provides a ﬁrst-order approximation of training speed by quantifying how well gradient updates computed for one minibatch generalize to other points in the training set.
label: none

sentence: In view of this link, the empirical and theoretical ﬁndings in recent work [14, 39], which show a notion of the variance of gradients over the training data is correlated with generalisation, become another piece of supporting evidence for training speed as a measure of generalisation.
label: none

sentence: Finally, [26] prove that, in the setting of linear models and inﬁnitely wide deep models performing Bayesian updates, the marginal likelihood, which is a theoretically-justiﬁed tool for model selection in Bayesian learning, can be bounded by a notion of training speed.
label: none

sentence: This notion of training speed is deﬁned as a sum of negative log predictive likelihoods, terms that resemble the losses on new data points seen by the model during an online learning procedure.
label: none

sentence: Maximising Bayesian marginal likelihood is also equivalent to minimising the PAC-Bayesian bound on the generalisation error as shown by [15].
label: none

sentence: In particular, this suggests that using the TSE approach for model selection in Bayesian models is equivalent to minimizing an estimate of a PAC-Bayes bound.
label: none

sentence: Because the NAS settings we consider in our experiments use neural networks rather than Bayesian models and due to space constraints, we defer the statement and proof of this result to Appendix A.
label: none

sentence: Training Speed Estimation The results described above suggest that leveraging a notion of training speed may beneﬁt model selection procedures in NAS.
label: none

sentence: Many such notions exist in the generalisation literature: [17] count the number of optimisation steps needed to attain a loss below a speciﬁed 2 threshold, while [16] consider the total number of optimisation steps taken.
label: none

sentence: Both measures are strong predictors of generalisation after training, yet neither is suitable for NAS, where we seek to stop training as early as possible if the model is not promising.
label: research_gap

sentence: We draw inspiration from the Bayesian perspective and the PAC-Bayesian bound discussed above and present an alternate estimator of training speed that amounts to the area under the model’s training curve.
label: none

sentence: Models that train quickly attain a low loss after few training steps, and so will have a lower area-under-curve than those which train slowly.
label: none

sentence: This addresses the shortcomings of the previous two methods as it is able to distinguish models both early and late in training.
label: none

sentence: We empirically show in Section 4.2 that our proposed TSE and its variants (TSE-E and TSE-EMA), despite their simple form, can reliably estimate the generalisation performance of neural architectures with a very small training budget, can remain effective for a large range of training epochs, and are robust to the choice of hyperparameters such as the summation window E and the decay rate γ.

sentence: However, our estimator is not meant to replace the validation accuracy at the end of training or when the user can afford large training budget to sufﬁcient train the model.

sentence: We show in Figure 1 and Appendix C that our proposed sum over training losses (TSE) outperforms the sum over validation losses (SoVL) in ranking models in agreement with their true test performance. 3 Related Work Various approaches have been developed to speed up architecture performance estimation, thus improving the efﬁciency of NAS.
label: none

sentence: Low-ﬁdelity estimation methods accelerate NAS by using the validation accuracy obtained after training architectures for fewer epochs (namely early-stopping) [23, 13, 53, 49], training a down-scaled model with fewer cells during the search phase [53, 34], or training on a subset of the data [18].
label: none

sentence: However, low-ﬁdelity estimates underestimate the true performance of the architecture and can change the relative ranking among architectures [12].
label: research_gap

sentence: This undesirable effect on relative ranking is more prominent when the cheap approximation set-up is too dissimilar to the full training [49].
label: none

sentence: As shown in Fig. 1 below, the validation accuracy at early epochs of training suffers low rank correlation with the ﬁnal test performance.
label: none

sentence: Another class of performance estimation methods trains a regression model to extrapolate the learning curve from what is observed in the initial phase of training.
label: none

sentence: Regression model choices that have been explored include Gaussian processes with a tailored kernel function [10], an ensemble of parametric functions [10], a Bayesian neural network [19] and more recently a ν-support vector machine regressor (ν-SVR)[3] which achieves state-of-the-art prediction performance [41].
label: none

sentence: Although these model-based methods can often predict the performance ranking better than their model-free early-stopping counterparts, they require a relatively large amount of fully evaluated architecture data (e.g. 100 fully evaluated architectures in [3]) to train the regression surrogate properly and optimise the model hyperparameters in order to achieve a good prediction performance.
label: research_gap

sentence: The high computational cost of collecting the training set makes such model-based methods less favourable for NAS unless the practitioner has already evaluated hundreds of architectures on the target task.
label: research_gap

sentence: Moreover, both low-ﬁdelity estimates and learning curve extrapolation estimators are empirically developed and lack theoretical motivation.
label: research_gap

sentence: Weight sharing is employed in one-shot or gradient-based NAS methods to reduce computational costs [32, 24, 43].
label: none

sentence: Under the weight-sharing setting, all architectures are considered as subnetworks of a supernetwork.
label: none

sentence: Only the weights of the supernetwork are trained while the architectures (subnetworks) inherit the corresponding weights from the supernetwork.
label: none

sentence: This removes the need for retraining each architecture during the search and thus achieves a signiﬁcant speed-up.
label: none

sentence: However, the weight sharing ranking among architectures often correlates poorly with the true performance ranking [45, 48, 50], meaning architectures chosen by one-shot NAS are likely to be sub-optimal when evaluated independently [50].
label: research_gap

sentence: In Section 4.4, we demonstrate that we improve the performance of weight sharing in correctly ranking architectures by combining our estimator with it.
label: none

sentence: The datasets we experiment with are: 10 • NASBench-201 [11]: the dataset contains information of 15,625 different neural archi- tectures, each of which is trained with SGD optimiser and evaluated on 3 different datasets: CIFAR10, CIFAR100, IMAGENET-16-120 for 3 random initialisation seeds.
label: none

label: none

label: none

sentence: The dataset is available at https://github.com/D-X-Y/NAS-Bench-201 with MIT License. • RandWiredNN: we produce this dataset by generating 552 randomly wired neural architec- tures from the random graph generators proposed in [42] and evaluate their performance on the image dataset FLOWERS102 [31].
label: none

sentence: We explore 69 sets of hyperparameter values for the random graph generators and for each set of hyperparameter values, we sample 8 randomly wired neural networks from the generator.
label: none

sentence: A randomly wired neural network comprises 3 cells connected in sequence and each cell is a 32-node random graph.
label: none

sentence: The wiring/connection within the graph is generated with one of the three classic random graph models in graph theory: Erdos-Renyi (ER), Barabasi-Albert (BA) and Watt-Strogatz (WS) models.
label: none

sentence: Each random graph model has 1 or 2 hyperparameters that decide the generative distribution over edge/node connection in the graph.
label: none

sentence: All the architectures are trained with SGD optimiser for 250 epochs and other training set-ups follow those in [24].
label: none

sentence: This dataset allows us to evaluate the performance of our simple estimator on hyperparameter/model selection for the random graph generator.
label: none

sentence: We will release this dataset after paper publication. • DARTS: DARTS search space [24] is more general than those of NASBench-201 and contains over 1018 architectures.
label: none

sentence: It’s also the most widely adopted space in NAS [53, 24, 8, 43, 44, 34, 22, 32, 37, 51].
label: none

sentence: Particularly, this search space comprises a cell of 7 nodes: the ﬁrst two nodes in cell k are the input nodes which equals to the outputs of cell k −2 and cell k −1 respectively.
label: none

sentence: The last node in the cell k is the output node which gives a depthwise concatenation of all the intermediate nodes.
label: none

sentence: The remaining four intermediate nodes are operation nodes take can take one out of eight operation choices.
label: none

sentence: An architecture from this search space is formed by stacking the cell 8 or 20 times.
label: none

sentence: We generate three DARTS architecture datasets; each dataset contains 150 20-cell architectures randomly sampled from the search space but follows a different training set-up.

sentence: Speciﬁcally, for the dataset used in Figure 2 (b) of main text, we use an initial learning rate of 0.025, a cosine-annealing schedule and a batch size of 96 (i.e. the setting for CIFAR10 complete training in [24].

sentence: Speciﬁcally, we compare our proposed estimators, TSE and TSE-E, computed with training losses against two equivalent variants of validation loss-based estimators: Sum of validation losses (SoVL) and that over the most recent epoch (SoVL-E with E = 1).
label: none

sentence: For each image dataset, we randomly sample 5000 different neural network architectures from the search space and compute the rank correlation between the true test accuracies (at T = 200) of these architectures and their corresponding TSE/TSE-E as well as SoVL/SoVL-E up to epoch T.
label: none

sentence: The results in Figure 6 in the Appendix show that our proposed estimators TSE and TSE-E using training losses clearly outperform their validation counterparts.
label: none

sentence: Another intriguing observation is that the rank correlation performance of SoVL-E drops signiﬁcantly in the later phase of the training (after around 100 epochs for CIFAR10 and 150 epochs for CIFAR100) and the ﬁnal test loss, TestL (T=200), also correlates poorly with ﬁnal test accuracy.
label: none

sentence: This implies that the validation/test losses can become unreliable indicator for the validation/test accuracy on certain datasets; as training proceeds, the validation accuracy keeps improving but the validation losses could stagnate at a relatively high level or even start to rise [28, 40].
label: none

sentence: This is because while 12 the neural network can make more correct classiﬁcations on validation points (which depend on the maximum argument of the logits) over the training epochs, it also gets more and more conﬁdent on the correctly classiﬁed training data and thus the weight norm and maximum of the logits keeps increasing.
label: none

sentence: This can make the network overconﬁdent on the misclassiﬁed validation data and cause the corresponding validation loss to rise, thus offsetting or even outweighing the gain due to improved prediction performance [40].
label: none

sentence: Training loss will not suffer from this problem.
label: none

sentence: While TSE-E struggles to distinguish architectures once their training losses have converged to approximately zero, this contributes to a much smaller drop in estimation performance of TSE-E compared to that of SoVL-E and only happens near a very late phase of training (after 150 epochs) which will hardly be reached if we want efﬁcient NAS using as few training epochs as possible.
label: limitation

sentence: Therefore, the possibility of network overconﬁdence under misclassiﬁcation is another reason for our use of training losses instead of the validation losses.
label: none

sentence: D TSE Estimator Hyperparameters Our proposed TSE estimators require very few hyperparameters: the summation window size E for TSE-E and the decay rate γ for TSE-EMA, and we show empirically that our estimators are robust to these hyperparameters.

sentence: This, together with the almost monotonic improvement of our estimator’s rank correlation score over the training budgets, supports our hypothesis discussed in Section 2 that training information in the more recent epochs is more valuable for performance estimation.

sentence: Note that TSE-E with E = 1 corresponds to the sum of training losses over all the batches in one single epoch.

sentence: Keywords Neural Topic Modeling · BERTopic · Focus Group Analysis · Model Validation · Reproducibility · Hyperparameter Optimization · Bootstrap Resampling · Text Mining 1 Introduction Topic modeling has emerged as a powerful computational approach for discovering latent thematic structures in large text corpora.
label: none

sentence: Originally developed for document organization and information retrieval [2], topic modeling techniques have found widespread application across diverse text types.
label: none

sentence: Early work focused on structured document collections such as news articles, scientific papers, and web pages [13, 31].
label: none

sentence: More recently, researchers have applied topic modeling extensively to social media platforms including Twitter [32, 27], Reddit [11, 40], and online forums [37, 7], as well as to customer reviews [41, 26] and open-ended survey responses [15].
label: none

sentence: Recent advances in transformer-based architectures have enabled neural topic models that leverage contextual embeddings rather than traditional bag-of-words representations, offering improved performance for short, noisy text common in social media [14, 10].
label: none

sentence: Despite this breadth of applications, most implementations target large-scale corpora where statistical inference benefits from thousands or tens of thousands of documents.
label: research_gap

sentence: Moreover, standard benchmarks and evaluation protocols emphasize either well-structured documents (e.g., 20 Newsgroups, scientific abstracts) or homogeneous short texts (e.g., tweets about specific events).
label: research_gap

sentence: This leaves open questions about topic modeling performance on small, heterogeneous conversational corpora where documents vary substantially in length and thematic focus, and where corpus size may comprise only hundreds of utterances. arXiv:2511.18843v2 [cs.CL] 2 Dec 2025 A Reproducible Framework for Neural Topic Modeling in Focus Group Analysis A PREPRINT Focus group discussions represent a particularly important yet computationally underexplored text type.
label: research_gap

sentence: Unlike social media posts, which are spontaneous and often brief, focus groups are structured conversations where participants engage in moderated dialogue following a semi-structured protocol.
label: none

sentence: Unlike customer reviews or survey responses, which target specific products or questions, focus groups explore open-ended topics through emergent conversation.
label: none

sentence: Focus groups are widely used across health research, market research, policy analysis, and user experience studies, generating rich textual data that captures nuanced perspectives through natural conversation.
label: none

sentence: Despite their methodological prevalence, focus group transcripts have received limited attention in the computational topic modeling literature, likely reflecting both the proprietary nature of such data and the traditional emphasis on manual thematic coding.
label: research_gap

sentence: Yet when research objectives include systematic synthesis across multiple sessions, geographic contexts, or longitudinal studies, computational approaches could augment traditional analysis by efficiently identifying thematic patterns while preserving opportunities for human interpretation.
label: none

sentence: This paper presents a systematic, reproducible framework for applying BERTopic [14], a neural topic model, to focus group discussion transcripts.
label: none

sentence: Using data from ten focus groups exploring HPV vaccine perceptions in Tunisia, we address four methodological objectives: (1) systematic exploration of hyperparameter configurations to understand their influence on model outcomes, (2) assessment of topic stability through bootstrap resampling to quantify robustness, (3) comparison with Latent Dirichlet Allocation to contextualize BERTopic’s performance against traditional approaches, and (4) validation of topic interpretability through independent human evaluation by domain experts.
label: none

sentence: While our application focuses on health discourse, the methodological framework and findings have broader implications for topic modeling of small, heterogeneous conversational corpora common across qualitative research domains.
label: none

sentence: Our work makes three primary contributions to computational text analysis methodology.
label: none

sentence: First, we develop and validate the first systematic framework specifically designed for topic modeling of focus group transcripts, demonstrating that transformer-based approaches can extract interpretable themes from conversational qualitative data when properly configured and validated.
label: none

sentence: Second, we show that BERTopic substantially outperforms LDA for this data type, achieving 18% higher coherence while discovering more interpretable topics, with human validation confirming that compu- tational coherence metrics successfully predict expert judgments.
label: none

sentence: Third, through transparent documentation of all modeling decisions, systematic evaluation across multiple quality dimensions, and rigorous comparison with traditional approaches, we contribute to the growing literature on reproducible practices in qualitative research.
label: none

sentence: To ensure full reproducibility, we provide complete code, evaluation scripts, hyperparameter configurations, and detailed documentation of all modeling decisions.
label: none

sentence: Code and anonymized data are available at .... 2 Related Work 2.1 Topic Modeling Approaches Topic modeling encompasses a family of statistical methods for discovering latent thematic structures in document collections.
label: none

sentence: Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) [2] established the foundational probabilistic framework for topic modeling, modeling documents as mixtures of topics and topics as distributions over words.
label: none

sentence: While LDA remains widely used [21], its bag-of-words assumption discards word order and contextual information.
label: none

sentence: BERTopic [14] represents a neural alternative, combining transformer-based sentence embeddings with UMAP di- mensionality reduction [29], HDBSCAN clustering [4], and class-based TF-IDF weighting.
label: none

sentence: Comparative studies show BERTopic produces competitive coherence relative to LDA [10], though performance depends significantly on hyperparameter choices.
label: none

sentence: Recent work [3] demonstrated that optimal configurations vary with corpus characteristics, underscoring the importance of systematic parameter exploration. 2.2 Stability and Quality Assessment Assessing topic model quality requires evaluating multiple dimensions, as different metrics capture distinct aspects of model performance.
label: none

sentence: Greene et al. [12] advocated for bootstrap stability analysis as a criterion for topic model selection, proposing that models producing stable partitions across resampled data represent more reliable thematic structures.
label: none

sentence: Stability is typically quantified using partition similarity measures such as Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) or Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) [20, 39].
label: none

sentence: However, these metrics measure fundamentally different aspects of clustering agreement.
label: none

sentence: ARI quantifies exact pairwise assignment agreement and is sensitive to cluster boundary variations [20], while NMI measures information structure preservation based on entropy [39].
label: none

sentence: Recent systematic evaluations have demonstrated that NMI and ARI can produce different algorithm rankings depending on corpus characteristics [35], indicating that neither metric is universally superior and selection should align with analytical goals. 2 A Reproducible Framework for Neural Topic Modeling in Focus Group Analysis A PREPRINT Semantic coherence, typically measured using the Cv metric [34], assesses whether topic words form interpretable semantic groups.
label: none

sentence: However, coherence and stability represent distinct and sometimes conflicting quality dimensions [18, 22].
label: none

sentence: Koltcov et al. [22] demonstrated empirically that models can exhibit high coherence while maintaining poor stability, underscoring the importance of evaluating both dimensions.
label: none

sentence: Furthermore, algorithmic metrics frequently conflict with human judgments of topic quality [19, 5], and different coherence measures can disagree on model rankings [1].
label: research_gap

sentence: Meaney et al. [30] demonstrate that different evaluation metrics often favor models of different complexity, indicating that no single metric captures all aspects of topic quality.
label: none

sentence: These findings underscore the importance of multi-faceted evaluation that includes expert validation alongside computational metrics. 2.3 Applications to Qualitative Research and Reproducibility Challenges Topic modeling has found increasing application in qualitative research across multiple domains.
label: none

sentence: Substantial work has applied these methods to social media health discourse, including COVID-19 discussions on Twitter [32] and HPV vaccination debates [9].
label: none

sentence: More recently, researchers have analyzed structured qualitative data including patient experience surveys [38], psychotherapy transcripts [24], interview data [17], and open-ended survey responses [15, 6].
label: none

sentence: These applications demonstrate topic modeling’s potential for efficiently identifying thematic patterns in qualitative data while highlighting methodological challenges including domain-informed preprocessing, handling conversational dynamics, and hierarchical topic organization [8].
label: none

sentence: However, reproducibility has emerged as a critical concern.
label: research_gap

sentence: Hagg et al. [16] conducted a scoping review of 68 LDA studies in psychological science and found that most provided insufficient methodological detail to reproduce analyses, and that results are highly sensitive to analytic decisions.
label: research_gap

sentence: This challenge is particularly acute for small, heterogeneous qualitative corpora where configuration choices can profoundly affect outcomes.
label: research_gap

sentence: The lack of standardized evaluation protocols and transparent reporting practices undermines confidence in topic modeling findings, especially when results inform practical decisions.
label: research_gap

sentence: These issues highlight the need for systematic hyperparameter exploration, multi-dimensional quality assessment, rigorous validation protocols, and transparent documentation of all modeling choices.
label: research_gap

sentence: Despite growing applications, we could find no prior work explicitly applying topic modeling to focus group discussion transcripts.
label: research_gap

sentence: This gap is notable: focus groups generate multi-party conversations where meaning emerges through interactive dialogue, differing substantively from both social media (spontaneous, brief posts) and individual interviews (single-voice narratives).
label: research_gap

sentence: The present study addresses this gap by developing and validating a systematic BERTopic framework for focus group analysis, with transparent reporting of all methodological decisions to support reproducibility and adaptation by other researchers. 3 Methodology We apply BERTopic to HPV vaccine perception focus groups conducted in Tunisia.

sentence: Gaps in Healthcare AI S&P Research.
label: none

sentence: While healthcare AI research has received unprecedented attention among biomedical communities, there is a limited amount of un- derstanding of the adversarial robustness of this technology in the context of medical applications.
label: research_gap

sentence: Among all the papers we surveyed from both computer science venues (including security and AI/ML venues) and biomedical venues, there is a limited amount of research work focusing on these sys- tems, with roughly 10-20 publications each year (Figure 1).
label: research_gap

sentence: Besides the difference in research volume, there is also a dis- connect between the security and the biomedical community in the assumed threat models and technologies under study.
label: research_gap

sentence: Given the increasing role AI plays in delivering healthcare solutions, we aim to identify this gap and contextualize the risks of AI applications in different healthcare sub-domains.
label: none

sentence: Our Methodology.
label: none

sentence: To understand the most pressing re- search need for healthcare AI, we surveyed 3,162 articles in the past 5 years in major medical journals (including but not limited to Nature, Science, Cell, Lancet, and New England Journal of Medicine).
label: none

sentence: Drawing from this exercise, we de- veloped the systematization of healthcare application of AIs, based on which, it then becomes possible to contextualize the threat model for the analysis of the security works.
label: none

sentence: To under- stand the current state-of-the-art of security and privacy for healthcare AI, we collected 101 articles from both the secu- rity venues (IEEE S&P, USENIX Security, ACM CCS, etc.) as well as the AI venues (NeurIPS, AAAI, CVPR, etc.) in the past 10 years (See Appendix A).
label: none

sentence: Building on these ar- ticles, we not only systematize the common threat models, but also create a taxonomy of existing attacks and defenses based on the healthcare application domains (Table 1 and Table 2).
label: none

sentence: Through this exercise, we highlight areas where there is limited understanding, and discuss future directions to safeguard these lifesaving technology.
label: none

sentence: To test our ﬁndings 1 regarding research opportunities in under-explored domains, we conducted proof-of-concept validations with attack ex- periments considering realistic threat models in healthcare.
label: none

sentence: Our systematization reveals several interest- ing insights into the current state of S&P research in health- care AI.
label: none

sentence: First, the current research is skewed toward cer- tain threat types.
label: research_gap

sentence: For example, 43.8% of surveyed studies focused on adversarial examples for evasion attacks, while only 8.2% addressed issues related to AI model availability.
label: research_gap

sentence: Furthermore, the healthcare domain being studied is highly unbalanced. 41.1% of healthcare AI S&P research focused on image-related diagnostic tasks, while other application domains, such as disease risk prediction, are largely over- looked (2%).
label: research_gap

sentence: Another emerging trend is the rapid rise of gen- erative AI in healthcare research, which has gained increas- ing attention in the biomedical community since 2020.
label: none

sentence: Al- though generative models raise new security risks for health- care providers, the security community has largely over- looked these concerns (Appendix B).
label: research_gap

sentence: These gaps point to numerous opportunities for future research, underscoring the need to extend security and privacy investigations into a broader range of healthcare AI application domains.
label: future_work

sentence: While there have been works systematiz- ing AI/ML research in network intrusion detection [116], security applications [6], explainability [119], accountabil- ity [17], and privacy [145], a uniﬁed view on the topic in healthcare settings is not yet available.
label: research_gap

sentence: To bridge the gaps, we aim to present a systematic survey unifying ex- isting works and propose a comprehensive framework that helps shed light on challenges and opportunities for future research.
label: none

sentence: (§2) • We provide a comprehensive systematization of current S&P research on healthcare AI in various application domains, pointing out challenges and opportunities for future research.
label: none

sentence: (§3 - §7) • We conducted proof-of-concept validation of research opportunities with tailored attack experiments in di- verse under-explored healthcare domains.

sentence: We speciﬁ- cally sought to explore the S&P risks of generative AI in healthcare, along with traditional ML methods and deep neural networks (DNN), through experiments to validate the reasoning of our insights.
